article: They can manifest with similar symptoms, and both can inform the other, but they are separate issues. Anxiety is created by stresses, internal or external, and is a sort of fear or worry; a sense of dread, sometimes about specific things or sometimes about life in general. Anxiety is what you might feel when you're about to give a speech before a crowd, or when you walk down a dark alleyway at 3AM and a group starts following you. A person with an anxiety disorder might feel this way all the time for no reason at all. ADHD is a disorder in the ability to direct and control mental focus. A healthy brain will automatically filter its experiences according to importance if you are reading a book, then a pigeon cooing in the background is unimportant, and you 'filter it out'. A gunshot going off, that's important, that will grab all of your attention instantly. If something reminds you of the dog you had as a child, that crosses your mind briefly, but you decide to ignore it and get back to reading. In an ADHD brain, that doesn't happen; the filter is weak or absent. The book you are reading is equally as important as the pigeon cooing; your attention will be divided equally among both. If a line in your book reminds you of Jimmy Stewart, you are now thinking equally about a French guy eating a madeleine and Jimmy Stewart's dialogue from Rope. And because the faculties for directing attention are already weakened, it isn't possible to consciously redirect this attention the way a normal person might when studying. Conversely, when a particular subject or idea is personally engaging and highly-attention-grabbing, it can be impossible to stop thinking about it a state called hyperfocus. This is why some ADHD patients will display 'savant' or 'stupid genius' behaviour by knocking off War Peace over a weekend but not being able to follow the plot of CSI. There are two predominant subtypes of ADHD. In Predominantly-Inattentive, or ADHD-PI, the attention-director in your brain says "Everything is equally important; focus equally on everything." Your attention is divided equally among every thought, emotion, sensation and experience occurring at this moment and in your short-term memory, becoming so diffuse that in extreme circumstances you have 'zoned out'. In Predominantly-Hyperactive, or ADHD-PH, the attention-director says "Nothing here is really important; go find something important." It's the same sensation a normal person would get when sitting in a doctor's waiting room, except it occurs 247 regardless of what is happening, resulting in the sufferer bouncing from activity to activity and thought to thought at a manic pace desperately looking for a non-existent stimulus that will be ranked as important. ADHD results in anxiety for almost all sufferers, because it makes many things, like studying material that isn't personally engaging, virtually impossible, making it difficult to direct or progress one's life, making it hard or impossible to attend schools or take many jobs this creates a strong sense of self-hatred among many ADHD patients, and self-harm and suicide rates are high (and for ADHD-PH, drug abuse rates are also very high). The medications that treat ADHD are also generally variations on amphetamines, and one of the primary symptoms of using them is anxiety.

article: Scratching causes irritation, irritation causes inflamation. Inflamation is the body's go-to reaction for anything it percieves as harmful (whether or not it actually is harmful) It's characterised by swelling,redness,pain, local increase of heat and some level of function loss for the affected tissue. The area is flooded with cells that aim to reduce and repair any potential damage, or mess you up if you have an auto-immune disease. Source: medstudent," "When you scratch your skin, you damage some of the cells present over there. When cells get damaged or injured they release certain chemicals called as inflammatory mediators. These inflammatory mediators cause inflammation over the area where they are released. The inflammation is characterised by 1. Redness 2. Swelling 3. Warmth 4. Pain Edit: 5. Loss of function Inflammation is body's defence against any injury to its cells. It serves by bringing more white blood cells (body's soldiers) to the site of injury.,A slightly more in depth explanation, more like ELI10 than 5: Inflammation is the one of the first levels of defense against infection: your body floods the area and, in general, if more fluid is flowing in than coming out it is much more difficult for bacteria to swim against a current. Because the current is going towards the infection it brings all of the good guys (white blood cells) with it and using a fancy chemical communication system the white blood cells call for more inflammation, increased temp, and extra help if need be like a Horn of Gondor. The cells with the quickest response to foreign invaders are Mast Cells and their carrion clarion cry is Histamine. This is because they evolved to work best against parasites. Parasites are usually much larger than a single white blood cell and they can't just be swallowed up and digested like bacteria so the best response to a parasite is to quickly make the environment as hostile as possible while stopping the invader from getting to a vital area. Whenever your body recognizes a parasite (or something it might think is a parasite) the mast cells release their histamine and the body's response is swift. Flood the area with fluid, all droids to battle stations. As a side note you've probably heard of histamines from allergy commercial or two. Seasonal allergies are your body mis-identifying large pollen molecules as scary parasites. Your body is effectively fighting an unnecessary war against something that cant actually hurt you. There is some thought that the lack of parasitic infections in modern society does not provide the appropriate training to the immune system and it gets bored and starts causing trouble (think of a standing army living on your land during peacetime). This is called the hygiene hypothesis. Lastly, you can literally cause a mast cell to release its contents just by squeezing. Your body doesn't know that there are no invaders and it has evolved to be quick and fast in its response because "better safe than sorry." Some people have a condition called dermatographia where they can literally write on their skin by scratching it because they have an extra release of histamine. A nice caveat is that whenever any cell is damaged it releases chemicals which, like a death wail, start reving up the immune system whether it was due to an infection or not. For example, when you twist an ankle your body starts responding to the deaddying cells of your tendons and soft tissue and you get a huge swollen, hot ankle even though there are no invaders present to warrant such a response. article: DSLR stands for digital single-lens reflex. These cameras use a silvered mirror or prism that redirects the image coming through the lens to the view finder. When the shutter is activated the mirrorprism snaps out of the way to allow the image to reach the image sensor. The advantage of this is that the image you see through the viewfinder is the exact image that the image sensor will "see." The other advantages of a DLSR are interchangeable lenses, a larger more sophisticated image sensor, and phase-detection autofocus. Point and shoot cameras sometimes come with interchangeable lenses, but the choice is limited and since the lenses are generally smaller, the quality is not as good. Point and shoots also usually use a contrast maximisation autofocus instead of phase-detection autofocus, which is quicker and more accurate. DSLT stands for digital single-lens translucent and is a proprietary system used by some Sony cameras. Instead of mirrorprism of the SLR, it uses a mirror that is partly silvered to split the image between the viewfinder and the image sensor. Some point and shoot digital cameras take very good pictures and they have the advantages of potability (you can't fit a DSLR into your pocket) and price.

You can read more about the phenomenon [here] (URL0),In anatomyphysiology, we call this "cavitation." This happens because of pressure changes inside your joints. Some background info: - Your joint is covered by a layer of tissue called the "synovium." Think of this as a layer of shrink wrap around your joints, essentially creating a capsule around your joint. - Your blood has the ability to carry dissolved gases, sort of like how a bottle of pop carries carbon dioxide gas. In the case of the human body, the dissolved gas in play here is nitrogen (which as a side note makes up almost 80 of the air we breathe). When you move a stiff joint, you actually create a change in pressure inside that synovium. That change in pressure it sort of like if you open a fresh bottle of soda. You know those bubbles that appear in the bottle? To a smaller extent, that's what also happens in your joints. This is because gas only dissolves in liquid at a certain pressure. If there's less pressure, then the gas will escape the fluid and become bubbles. The popping noise you hear is a bubble forming in your joint and then popping as the pressure normalizes and gets reabsorbed into the blood stream. The popping noise is what we call "cavitation." (Other possible causes for popping in joints, but somewhat less common, is tight tendons rubbing up against each other, or friction against bone surfaces in the case of cartilage wearing down - but if you're thinking of your knuckles cracking, 99 likely it's the cavitation phenomenon causing it.) article: Bicycle (and motorcycle) dynamics are very complex. Physicists and mathematicians have been having trouble modeling exactly what makes two wheeled vehicles stable. [Here's] (URL5) one stab at it. Some things are known to increase stability. The gyroscopic effect of the wheels plays a minor role. As [ubjujey] (URL4) pointed out below, experiments have shown that removing the gyroscopic effect still makes for a stable bike. Trail also plays a role. Trail is the measurement of where the steering axis in relation to the contact of the wheel on the ground. [Here's] (URL0) a picture for illustration. This is also called the caster effect. Basically the further forward the steering axis is from wheel contact with the ground, the more stable the bike. Track bikes and cyclocross bikes have really short trail to make them more agile. Big stable cruisers have long trails. Like gyroscopic effect, experiments have removed trail as a variable and these models are also stable. [Here] (URL3) is an interview with a scientist who removed both gyroscopic and castertrail effects in a model bicycle, and it remained stable. tl;dr: No one really knows what makes a moving bike stable. article: There are two main ways to try to estimate this. One is to start with the total number of positions. So you start with that number, then start pairing it down, eliminating positions with more than 32 pieces, more than one king to a side, etc., until you have as low of an upper bound as possible. The other way is to make estimates like there are about 30 legal moves in typical position, a typical game has 45 moves to a side, and try to refine things from there. article: Durability would suffer. Air compresses. This allows the tire to deform and then return to it's original shape much more easily. It also allows the tire to deform slightly to create a contact patch along the bottom and it rolls over uneven ground. Also I've never encountered a rubbery material that wouldn't eventually retain some impression of it was compressed long enough. I could see them developing flat spots along the bottom if a vehicle was stored for too long. Weight is also a factor. Unsprung weight (aka tires and some suspension components, brakes etc) are detrimental to handling. Let's say you hit a pothole. The tire drops into the hole a bit, and then rebounds upward as it hits the side on the way out. The heavier the wheel and tire is the further it is going to be launched upward before the suspension can dampen out the movement, and push it back down to the road. This is only a fraction of a second, but during that time you've got one wheel that isn't gripping the road. If it happens during hard cornering, it could be the difference between losing control or not. I could go on, but I'll end with this. Will someone eventually develop a tire that works better than what we're currently using? I'm sure they will, but it'll be tough to make it work well and be as cost effective, as what we now use. article: You'll need to be more specific about which'flat map'. It's affected by your choice of map projection. But I believe for a standard Mercator projection no, flying due east (except at the equator) isn't a great circle and you're flying along a line of constant latitude.,A straight line on a globe appears as a curve on a flat map, since projecting the curved earth on a flat image creates distortion. I think that more or less answers your question.','If you used a compass to fly in any direction, it would be a straight line on a Mercator projection. Other projections, it depends (due east, west, north, or south would probably be straight lines on a lot of maps but again, it depends). In a Mercator projection, "rhumb lines" are straight lines. A rhumb line is the path you would take if you maintained a constant compass heading (important for naviation). As your latitude changes, a constant heading actually points in a slightly different direction because you are getting closer to the magnetic pole. Ever wonder why Mercator projections never show the North or South Pole? They can't - a rhumb line that isn't due north or south will theoretically spiral around the pole forever, so the poles are at positive and negative infinity... A Lambert projection has the pole at the center and the lines of latitude are circles around it. This projection has the characteristic that Great Circles are straight lines. You can't show the equator on a Lambert projection because it would be infinite distance from the pole (because the equator, being a great circle, would have to be a straight line....) ','The shortest distance between two points on a globe follows the path of a circle around the circumference of that globe, connecting those two points. While not answering your first question, this is why looking at a flight path appears arced on a map. So the flight path is not "due east." If you followed a compass due east, walking or flying, you would appear to make a straight line on a standard map, but at least by air you would not be taking the shortest route to your destination.

It's also worth mentioning that since the power plants would still need fuel to generate electricity, someone would have to pay for it. That means taxes, so really, you would be paying for your electricity either way. If you wantneed more information, feel free to ask. "Energy is conserved" is quite literally the foundation of physics. second edit: Tesla's method was supremely inefficient. It suffered from "radius-squared loss" which is an issue common to any wireless transmission method, and it relied on the Earth as a conductor, and the Earth frankly sucks as a conductor, which means loss. It might work, but there have been hundreds of thousands of engineers and physicists that have looked over Tesla's work on wireless power, and you'll very rarely see any of them promoting it. article: The square-cube law limits the sizes of things. If you make a creature ten times longer then it will have a hundred times the surface area (square law) but a thousand times the weight and volume (cube law). For insects, which absorb air through their skin (they have no lungs) this means that big insects can't absorb enough oxygen through their skin to support their much larger volume. Strength also scales with the square but has to support a body weight that scales with the cube. And there are many other similar issues that place limits on any life form.,If your reference is the length of the animal with legs included, there are. Snow crabs can get HUGE. The bigger picture is that exoskeletons are inefficient, because they supply a limited area to attach things (organs, muscles) to. You can attach things to all sides of a bone, but only to the inside of a shell. Another aspect is that no known crustacean has evolved lungs, they all rely on fairly primitive (read: inefficient) forms of gills, which limits their body size as well. Finally, molting (sloughing off the old exoskeleton and forming a new one, which is required for the animal to grow) becomes harder and harder the larger the animal in question gets. At some point, a molt will fail and the animal will die.','Not sure how big you want but the Japanese Spider Crab is freaky big. article: Filibustering is a tactic that evolved in the Senate. It's often called a "parliamentary procedure," as it results not from constitutional law but the internal rules of the legislature. In order to allow time for a bill to be discussed and debated, a 60 vote majority is required to proceed from discussion to a vote. Senators realized they could exploit this rule to keep the majority from passing a bill, unless they had a 60-vote majority (a "Fillibuster-proof majority." Filibusters used to require a significant investment of time. Senators grew weary of the pain of a filibuster, and today, the mere threat of a filibuster is enough to get a bill withdrawn due to the time involved Senators in the past were known to read recipes, Shakespeare, anything in sight] (URL0 Now, to your questions: Why is it valid? Because it works for the minority party. Why is it not simply dismissed? No majority will eliminate it because they know it will be useful to them in the future. You'll hear of the "Nuclear Option" from time to time, a threat to eliminate the filibuster by changing the rules (by simple majority). So far, it has not happened. I wouldn't be surprised to see it happen in the next congress - the rise of use of filibuster is unprecedented (the filibuster itself is less than 100 years old) and scorched-earth politicking has become more and more common inside the beltway. Does it have any practical uses? Yes: It's a tool for the minority party to block particularly controversial legislation.', "The point is to make sure that a tightly-knit majority doesn't run roughshod over the minority. It is, by design, a stalling tactic to try and put the brakes on the discussion until the minority thinks there has been sufficient debate. Originally you had to actually filibusterthat is, get up and talk (the way that Rand Paul and Ted Cruz did fairly recently), but the Senate has expanded its use to allow Senators to just declare that they are filibustering. Ultimately the check on its use is in overuseif you use it too often, you and your party start to develop a bad name and lose even more seats. article: The human voice doesn't just come from the vibration of the vocal cords, but from the resonances of the chest, throat, nasal cavity, and mouth. When you're singing you're letting out a lot more air from a now much more open resonant chamber, and need to have much more precise breath control and vocal placement to hit the notes properly. article: Think of entropy as chaos. Disorder. If I took a pack of cards, there's only one way the pack can be entirely in order, so the entropy is low. If I shuffle it a little bit, the entropy increases, and it increases more the more I shuffle it - that is, there are lots of possible ways for the cards to be arranged, so the entropy is high. This is also why your room seems to get messier; a chaotic room is entropically favoured over a tidy, ordered room. It's why your headphones always seem to tangle themselves in your pocket - they can only be tidy one way, and massively tangled in potentially billions of ways. The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of a system will spontaneously increase. Spontaneously here means'without someone giving it a helping hand'. Your room can return to a lower entropic state, if you put energy into tidying it. You can untangle your headphones, but this takes energy. A slightly more advanced example is that solids have a lower entropy than liquid, as the atoms are all stuck in place, as opposed to liquids where the atoms can flow around one another, like balls in a ball pit. Obviously, gases have a higher entropy still. TL,DR: Entropy is disorder.,Have you ever built a house of cards? You start stacking cards on top of each other, one by one, slowly increasing the size of the structure. It takes you a lot of time and energy, but you finally finish. Just as you are about to take a picture, your little brother comes in and knocks it over. The structure that took you hours to build is destroyed in a matter of seconds. This is entropy- energy must be spent to create order from chaos, and since chaos is easier to maintain than order, things tend towards chaos.', "1st Law of Thermo: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. 2nd Law of Thermo: Entropy So lets say you drop a dictionary. It falls, hits the ground, and stops. When it was falling, it had kinetic energy. When it stops, that energy must have gone somewhere, and it goes into heat and sound. But why can't the reverse happen? Why can't I heat up the floor a smidge, set a dictionary on the floor, yell at it, and have the dictionary fly up into the air? That's entropy. Entropy says that the kinetic energy that the dictionary had is happier being heat and sound, so it won't go back into moving the dictionary.,Entropy is a measure of ignorance. Suppose you have a system with N possible states. You know that it is in state number 7. The probability that it is in state number 7 is 1; the probability that it is in any other state is 0. The entropy is 0. Some time later you don't know anything about the state of the system. The probability that the system is in any state is 1N. The entropy is at its maximum. There is a derivation I read in some physics textbook that says that the only formula in concord with the intuitive notion "measure of ignorance" and some reasonable assumptions is: H - S p log p where the summation is done over all the states of the system, and p is the probability of each state.','Brian Cox explained it in a pretty simple way. Hopefully this is viewable to the rest of the world. URL0

article: Although killing bacteria is definitely a big deal, the most important thing about cooking is that it breaks down complex proteins, called denaturing. Proteins are very complex, and breaking them down into usable chunks takes energy. There are also complex sugars, like cellulose, that are just too big for us to digest without breaking them down a little first. That's why herbivores usually spend almost their entire day foraging, and why carnivores spend most of the day doing nothing. Energy is precious, animals can't afford to waste it. Herbivores need to eat constantly to get the energy they need and carnivores have to save what they have to spend it catching more food later. Humans, on the other hand, get way more usable energy out of food. Modern farming aside, we barely spend any time eating, and we get a huge boost of energy very soon after we eat. What do we do with all that extra energy? We get smarter. Human brains use a ridiculous 20 of our energy to fuel our brains. No animal comes close to that. And that massive energy expenditure is only possible because we cook our food first. It was certainly discovered by accident, probably animals caught in fires, or pre-humans using fire for light and heat accidentally dropped food in. It likely smelled pretty good. Over time and evolution, humans who favored the smell of cooked meat got more calories and reproduced. Mind, that's speculation, because we don't know for sure. That's also the opposite of the usual story, which is that pre-humans got smart and learned how to cook, rather than discovering cooking to get smart. article: Chess is actually very predictable game, at least compared to some. There are only 64 squares. There are only two players. A maximum of 32 pieces. Those 32 pieces are of 6 types, and each type has rigid limits on how it can move. The starting position of every piece and every type is pre-determined and always the same, so there is very little variation in opening moves (to the point where even humans can memorize all of the possible board variations after the first two moves, because there's only a few hundred). And the entire board is visible at once, so every player knows the position of ever game piece. Also, chess is a game of reduction: over the course of the game, pieces are removed from the board, which reduces the total number of possible moves as the game progresses. There are never more than the starting 32 pieces. A lot of what chess AI's have traditionally done is brute force computation of all the possible moves several moves ahead and ranking of those outcomes. They can do that because chess is more predictable than other games. Now, compare this to something like Civilization. There are thousands of hexes on a Civilization map. There are as few as two and as many as a dozen (?? maybe it's less, I don't recall) players, human and AI. There is no real maximum number of game pieces (although there's probably a computational limit determined by the computer's processing power). There are dozens, if not hundreds, of different types of game pieces, each of which might have a different combination of moves and attack power. The starting positions of every piece is not predetermined, so you never know where on the game map an opponent will start or will add new pieces to the game. And most of the game field is unknown for most of the game. And new pieces can be added: the game is additive, with new pieces being added all the time (even as a players overall force is being reduced), meaning that the number of possible moves increases much more rapidly than in a game like chess, particularly in mid-game. tl;dr Chess is simple, so AI's can learn it. Civilization is way more complex, so AI's have to cheat to be smarter than humans.," "The goal of AI in a computer game isn't to win - it's to present a calibrated challenge to the player. However, if you were to attempt to design the'perfect' AI for a game like Civilization you'd first need to determine what that perfect strategy should look like. Lacking the millennia of thought about the rules of the game as you have with Chess, this would be a fairly difficult task with little reward - especially considering you'd need to redo all your work whenever a new version came out.,You are making a lot of assumptions about the similarity between both AI and in the game they are playing. article: A traditional bank offers two services: Loans and savings. Loans are where the bank will lend money to a person or business, who will then pay the money back to the bank (plus interest). Savings are where a person or business will ask a bank to hold onto their money for them and the bank will pay them interest over time. The money that banks use for loans is the money deposited by people saving with bank. Banks make money by charging a higher interest rate on loans than they pay out to savers. For example, a bank might ask for 6 interest on a PS100 loan and then pay 1 interest on a savings account with PS100. This means that the bank will make PS5 in profit. Investment banking is quite different. An investment bank offers advisory services to businesses looking to "float" themselves on the stock market. The investment bank can also buy all of a company's shares when they are issued and sell them to investors on the company's behalf (saving the company a lot of time and effort with finding investors). The investment bank makes money by selling the shares for a higher amount than they paid for them. As investment banking is based on a lot of speculation (trying to predict changes in the market), it's inherently risky. If an investment bank buys 10,000 shares in a company at PS20 each, it could sell them for PS25 (25 profit) each if it correctly predicts the market but it could also get it wrong and have the shares be worth less on the market than what they paid for them.

article: The potassium and sodium ion concentrations are what cause the neuron to fire. Or actually they allow the action potential to propagate along the nerve. A nerve cell starts off at a resting state with a negative charge inside and positive charge outside the cell membrane. When a signal is received, sodium ions rush into the cell causing a rapid depolarization and a shift to a positive charge inside the cell. This then triggers the opening of potassium ion channels, allowing potassium ions to flow out of the cell, which repolarizes the cell back to a negative charge again. This movement of ions creates an electrical signal that travels along the length of the neuron, allowing for the transmission of the signal from one neuron to the next.

article: It's because rear view mirrors have more than one reflecting surface. There is a flat mirror, of course, but in front of it there is also a wedge-shaped prism (just a wedge shaped piece of glass really) that tilts slightly down. This front surface is not that great of a reflector, so you don't notice it during the day. Light goes right through and you get a strong reflection out of the good old mirror. During the night, bright headlights behind you can make it hard to see, so you can tilt the mirror such that the reflection off the prism is what you see (and the mirror instead reflects the light upward so it's not in your eyes). And since the prism is not very good at reflecting, the headlights behind you are dimmer. I assume you only turn the light on in your car when it is dark outside. Thus, there is a good chance your mirror is tilted in the "dimmed" position, where the front (less reflecting) surface is point out the back window, and the mirror is thus pointing toward your ceiling light. Turn the light on, and it reflects off the back surface (mirror) and into your eyes.

article: Irony is a part of satire, so we'll start with irony. There are a couple forms of irony: Dramatic irony is a situation in which the audience knows something that the characters in the story or play do not. For example, in Shakespeare's play "Romeo and Juliet," the audience knows that Juliet is not really dead, but Romeo does not, which creates tension and tragic irony when he kills himself. Another form of irony is situational irony, where the outcome is opposite of what was expected. A classic example of situational irony is a fire station burning down. Something we typically think of as providing safety ends up causing the very thing it was designed to prevent. Verbal irony is another form of irony, where someone says something but means the opposite. For example, if it's raining outside and someone says, "what a beautiful day!" Satire often employs irony to poke fun at or criticize something. The satirist might use dramatic irony to show how foolish a character is or use situational irony to point out the flaws in a particular system or belief. The US Constitution has a set of amendments (the first ten, ratified way back in 1791) called the Bill of Rights. These have come to define a central part of the American concept of civil rights. One of these amendments is the 2nd Amendment, which sets aside a specific right to bear arms that "shall not be abridged." This amendment was originally demanded by anti-federalists in order to fulfill two roles; to make sure the citizenry would be appropriately armed to serve in militias, and to make sure that these militias would be well armed enough to challenge the federal government should it become necessary. At the time, this was a rather practical measure, since not only was gun ownership very common, but it was also a requirement for many people. Moreover, at the time republics of the sort they were experimenting with had essentially never really existed before and the anti-federalists didn't trust that the federal government being established by the Constitution would stay within its legal boundaries. So they demanded the 2nd amendment as a measure to assure that the government would not disarm the populace, and enable them to resist the government if required (which was a lot more feasible back then, since the US federal government was a weak and uncertain thing in 1791). Anyway, the social context of the United States has changed greatly in the intervening 200 years. We're now an advanced industrial state with a huge standing military, no need for militias, and a largely urban population contending with new issues like mass gun violence and suicide rather than threats that our now well established federal government is going to turn into some apocalyptic tyranny. But yet the 2nd amendment remains, and it prevents the federal government from taking any effective legal measures to reduce gun violence in the United States. The arguments that result are mainly about one group of people (the pro-gun-control group) who want to update statutory law to be more reflective of prevailing American society and concerns by imposing some level of gun control, and another group of anti-gun-control proponents who want to preserve a strict individual right to bear arms according to the 2nd amendment. This is the source of the tension, and currently this has been brought to a head by a rash of mass shootings that have captured popular attention, inflaming both sides. The pro-control side sees this as an example of everything they've been fighting to prevent for decades, and the anti-gun side now fears more than ever that the government is going to go grabbing guns, so they're arming up in record numbers.','The 2nd Amendment of the constitution reads: "A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed." article: Basically, SN1 favors stability, and SN2 favors a quick attack. If you have a large structure with many carbons attached to it, andor with many conjugated bonds (which also increase stability) See benzene, SN1 will likely be favored thermodynamically. There are still reactions with SN2 models on larger compounds, but they are less common and will probably not be tested over. SN2 would not be favored in the in large bulky compounds because of steric hindrance. SN2 does that back attack thing remember? It likes to shoot in really fast and not bump into anything on it's way. SN2 favors a strong nucleophile (negatively charged) which basically attacks the nucleus (positively charged) quickly. There are reactions that you can do at low temperatures that will favor SN1 because of it's love for stability and a thermodynamically favorable product, but will favor SN2 at high temperatures. Why? Well SN2 is fast and doesn't care about stability, and SN1 is slow and careful. Edit: To clarify this section, slowing down the reaction will favor the formation of thermodynamically stable products, while speeding up a reaction favors the product that forms most quickly. So in a most basic sense, if you see a very stable molecule andor a weak nucleophile, it will be SN1. If you see a unstable molecule as you carbo-cation andor a strong nucleophile (strong base in most cases) it will be SN2 because a quick reaction will take place. Solvent is also important, but I can't go into that because it's been too long. Something about polar proticaprotic or something. Good luck and I hope that helps clear things up.

article: The music is already mastered for a set of studio speakers in a studio that can accurately reproduce the audio. When you listen to music on your phone, you're using a very crappy phone speaker, or an equally crappy set of ear-bud speakers. These speakers can't reproduce the full range of audio that is described in the audio file. Speakers best reproduce frequencies related to their size. 12in. subwolfers are used to reproduce base, because they're large enough to match the long wavelengths of bass sounds. a 1in tweeter is used to reproduce treble, because the small speaker size matches the higher pitches. Your phone earbuds are effectively tweeters, and so can't produce the lower notes with the fidelity that a larger speaker could. Software equalizers let you partially compensate for the deficiencies of your speakers. It lets you adjust the different frequency ranges to better fit your speaker's abilities. Software EQs also lets you compensate for effects of your surroundings. I can have the best speakers in the world, and still need to EQ my audio. article: In theory, anything that isn't encrypted. If you're using a website with HTTPS you should be fine, although a bad guy might still be able to see the fact that you're connecting to that website. If you need more security than that, consider a VPN.,The answer is "It depends on your ISP" When DOCSIS (the protocol on which the cable modem talks back to your ISP) was first introduced, there was no encryption on the data between your modem, and the ISP. DOCSIS being a radio frequency protocol (just constrained inside the wire) is based on broadcasts, and the modems were set to just ignore everything that was not addressed to you. This meant that anyone on your node, which is usually most or all of your entire neighborhood, could hook a modified device up to the cable plant and listen to everything that everybody else in the neighborhood did that was not through HTTPS. DOCSIS version 1.1 introduced something called BPI, or Baseline Privacy Interface, the is what is important here. The original DOCSIS had something called BPI which is part of what told each modem the 'address' to listen for, and BPI added encryption to each individual modem using a key exchange much in the same way that HTTPS uses SSL (This was originally 56bit DES, and has since been improved to 128bit AES in BPI SEC which was introduced with DOCSIS 3.0) Now here is the tricky part, and why the answer still is "It Depends on your ISP." All of the encryption features are completely optional, and are not enabled by default. They are quite simple to implement (on the ISP side) and I don't personally know of any ISPs that are not running at least the 56bit DES version of BPI on their plants (as it also helps prevent theft of service), I am sure there are a few out there that have not enabled it.

article: Interpol doesn't actually investigate anything or have any jurisdiction. It just facilitates contact between police departments in different countries. For example, lets say you're a police officer in Chicago who is investigating a criminal that fled overseas, but you don't know where. Without Interpol it would be very difficult, if not impossible to find that person. With Interpol you can send them your warrant and they will then put the warrant into a database that other nation's law enforcement agencies check against. So your criminal tries to cross an international border somewhere. When they do that, the local customs agents will check them against Interpol's database, discover that they are wanted in Chicago, and then arrest them so they can be extradited. It also helps out in investigations between different countries. Again, lets say you're investigating a human trafficking ring that spans multiple countries. Without Interpol it would be difficult to impossible to know what other countries also had law enforcement working on the same case as you, and you would have similar troubles figuring out who to contact in those countries even if you did find out they were conducting a parallel investigation. With Interpol, you can send them a notice giving them a rough outline of what you're investigating and they will check that against what other law enforcement agencies are also telling them. If Interpol sees that both you and a law enforcement agency in another country are investigating the same thing, they'll put you in contact with one another. Likewise, if you want an investigation started in another country Interpol will know who to put you in contact with to get that started.," "Yeh Interpol itself doesn't have officers, or agents that they send around to do police work, it's essentially an organisation to allow different police forces around the world to work together. article: When you connect the two batteries together, does it close a circuit and create one giant battery? Essentially, yes, although the dead battery doesn't contribute much, the live battery is doing all the work. And when dead car starts, is it just drawing power from the giant battery? On the car's motor is running, it is driving the alternator, which charges the battery. Let it run for 10, 15 minutes, and it should have enough juice to start up again.,Sounds like someone is preparing for the Canadian winters.','When you connect the jumper cables between the batteries, you do indeed create one larger battery by connecting the batteries in parallel. But, the battery in the dead car is drained, so only the battery in the other car will contribute when starting. As soon as you connect the cables, the generator in the running car will start to charge the battery in the dead car. Depending a lot on the quality of the jumper cables, you can either start the dead car straight off of the other cars battery. If that doesn't work, you're most likely using low quality cables that have too great of a resistance, which creates a voltage loss when a current is drawn, not being able to provide enough power to the starting car. In that case, just let the "other car" run for 10 minutes (with elevated idling, around rpm is good) while connected, and it's alternator will charge the battery in the dead car. It won't be fully charged in 10 minutes, but because it has charged a bit, less current has to be drawn through the jumper cables since the starter can now use current from that battery too. Less current also means less voltage drop over the cables, providing even more power. So why won't low quality cables allow you to jump start a car directly without charging first? It's because the wires are so thin, and connected so poorly, that the cable has a quite high resistance. Since VIR, higher resistance equals higher voltage loss. When buying jumper cables, always buy the best quality you can find. You can also always double up cables. It's much better to have two pairs of low quality cables connected, than just one pair. Also, when connecting jumper cables, always make sure the clamps get as good of a connection as possible! This is very important, this frequently makes the difference between a successful and unsuccessful jump start. This means, don't just clamp them on and leave them, but pry the handles apart (so the clamps clamp with more force) and rotate the clamp back and forth a bit so it "digs in" a little bit. Sometimes it's necessary to actually have someone holding the cables, he should then try to pry the handles on the jumper cables apart, so they exert more force and "digs in" harder in the metal.

article: MRI magnets work by switching powerful electromagnets magnets on and off. They also have a 2nd super powerful magnet which is always on. When the electromagnets are turned on and off, they attract or repel each other and the always-on magnet. This attractionrepulsion causes vibrations which you hear as sounds. (This is basically how a loudspeaker works - you have a magnet, and an electromagnet connected to the speaker cone - you put an electrical signal into the electromagnet and it attractsrepels the other magnet moving the cone). Most types of scan with MRI make a sort of clunking or buzzing noise, but certain types (with strange names like diffusion weighted imaging, or functional imaging) make extremely loud beeping sounds, because the electromagnets are turned on and off so quickly that they produce a high frequency sound. It is possible to have much quieter sounds, by sequencing the electromagnets to only turn on and off gradually. This way, you don't get sudden attractionrepulsion which causes the big vibrations. Most scanners have an option to run in "silent" mode, with certain limitations (scan takes longer, images not as sharp, diffusion weighted imaging not available, etc.) There is a 2nd source of noise on most MRI scanners, which is much quieter and always on, which sounds like a strange little birdy tweeting - a sort of rhythmic tick-whoo-tick-whoo. This is the special cooler needed for the main magnet. The main magnet needs to be cooled to a low temperature (about -271 C), and it uses a special device called a Gifford-McMahon cooler which makes this strange pulsing noise. This actually makes noise from moving parts (it's the only moving part, apart from stuff like ventilation fans and the slider on the table).', "The magnetic forces generated inside an MRI machine are very difficult to appreciate, they are ginormous. The machine itself is flexed by the forces. It can't be made of thicker steel, because steel has magnetic properties. Any conductive metal can cause problems with the image, and so the machine has a lot of plastic structures that resonate with wonderful thumping sounds when the machine innards press on them.," "It's either spin the patient or the magnets. After early trials of spinning patients.... they quickly learned spinning the magnets was better.," "Finally one of these I have 1st hand experience with! There's a giant magnet inside an MRI machine that's cooled by liquid hydrogen. When a current is run through this magnet, the magnetic force generated is so strong that the coil of the magnet expands slightly. This expansion happens suddenly and is quite loud. Source: writes code for MRI image reconstruction

article: Simple probability, like what you'd use for a coin flip, doesn't care about previous outcomes. After 2 coin flips coming up heads the next one is still 50:50. You could try to logic your way into claiming that the next one will more likely be heads since you're on a streak of heads, or you could try to logic your way into claiming the next one will likely be tails because the streak has to end sometime. article: Red, green, and blue (RGB) are the primary colors for light (i.e., additive color). In this case, "black" is the absence of any light, and "white" is 100 of all three colors. Cyan, yellow, and magenta (CYM) are the primary colors for pigment (i.e., substractive color). In this case, "white" is the absence of any pigment, and "black" is 100 of all three pigment colors. Each of these pigments get their color from absorbing one of the primary light colors, and reflecting the other two. Thus cyan is the mix of green and blue (absorbs red), yellow is the mix of red and green (absorbs blue), and magenta is the mix of red and blue (absorbs green). The "K" in CYMK is "black." Printers will often add a separate reservoir of black ink for darker shades of color and for black white printing. EDIT: Bolded some terms and added language for clarity.

The First Amendment to the United States Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and prohibits the government from establishing or endorsing any particular religion. The "free exercise" clause protects an individual's right to practice their religion without interference from the government, while the "establishment" clause prohibits the government from establishing an official religion or promoting one religion over others. The phrase "separation of church and state" comes from a letter written by Thomas Jefferson in 1802 to the Danbury Baptist Association in which he used the phrase to explain his belief in the importance of keeping the government and religion separate.

article: There is plenty of'decorative' concrete that has pigments added, or more commonly, is stained or etched with acids after the concrete has been poured. But to properly color concrete, you need to use integral color. Integral color is a type of pigment that is mixed into the concrete before it is poured, resulting in a more even and long-lasting color throughout the entire slab or structure. It is available in a variety of colors and can be tailored to match any design or aesthetic preference. Integral color is typically added to the concrete at the batching plant or by a contractor on-site, and it is important to ensure that the color is mixed thoroughly to achieve an even appearance. Using integral color also eliminates the need for staining or etching, simplifying the maintenance and upkeep of the concrete surface.

Furthermore, your genes mutate, and those mutations either show up or they don't. As such, you likely have some weird mutated genes that would be really bad if they were dominant, but they aren't. I think that's how it goes. Comment by user: PatAunces saved on Tue Mar 08 2011 12:57:42 GMT-0500 (Eastern Standard Time) ','Your genes come in pairs. You get one from each parent. article: Apples just have a lot of variance. There are literally tens of thousands of different varieties of apples and if you grow apples from seeds you will get some of those random varieties. Most of them taste pretty bad. Modern apple farmers get a consistent product by essentially cloning one good type of apple tree over and over again through a process of grafting. If you wanted to have a delicious apple tree you would need to grow a tree from your seeds, get a crappy tree, and then graft a good trees branch onto it to grow good apples. tldr; you won't definitely get bad apples growing from seed but its very likely.," "The apple itself is genetically identical to the tree the apple is growing on. article: It basically comes down to making smaller transistors. The more transistors you can pack onto a chip, the more it can do. You make smaller transistors by discovering and developing better production methods. As you make the processes better, you can work in smaller and smaller spaces. Hard drives are a little different because there you're talking about packing more magnetic data closer, but again it really comes down to coming up with better manufacturing that lets you do that.,About every 18 months, we can implement the same functions in a silicon integrated circuit "chip" as before but in 12 the silicon area. Since the circuit area is approximately related to the minimum feature size in both the X and Y directions, and Area X times Y, this is similar to saying that every 18 months the feature sizes are reduced by a factor of 0.7x. (0.7 x 0.7 0.49.) In other words, a 30 improvement nets a 50 reduction in size. (Hard disc drives actually improve at an even faster rate.) How is this 30 improvement every 18 months accomplished? By lots of research, experimentation and hard work by a lot of people in a lot of disciplines. Materials science, electrical engineering, mechanical engineering, chemistry, optics, etc. all have a role to play to overcome the obstacles that arise from trying to cram more and more transistors into smaller and smaller areas. If it was just a matter of making the transistors smaller without changing anything else, it would proceed a lot faster. But every time you make the transistors smaller, it creates a bunch of new problems that were never solved before, or weren't solved to the degree that is now necessary. All of this kind of improvement has to happen at every process "node" or "generation," and usually a lot of experiments have to be run to find what will work and what won't. Fortunately, over the history of semiconductors a huge amount has been learned, and so we just continue to build upon that knowledge. And because the industry creates more and more powerful computers, it can USE more and more powerful computations to help in this work. Why doesn't this work go even faster than it already does? Because doing all of that work takes time and money, and the industry already invests as much money in R D as makes good business sense. With more resources it could go faster, but companies have to balance how much money they spend on R D versus all the other things they have to spend money on. If they strike the wrong balance, they get beaten by the competition and go out of business. It's like playing SimCity....you can't put all of your money into building new sports stadiums. To some extent, the rate of improvement is now a "self-fulfilling prophecy." Companies expect to improve at this rate, and put a lot of resources in place to make sure that they can, so they don't get beat by the competition. But a company that has a LOT of resources can apply the same percentage to R D and get a LOT more done. And in some cases, that happens. Intel is at least one process generation ahead of everyone else right now. Also, some of the experiments that need to be run simply take time to do. You could do more if you ran more experiments in parallel, but that would obviously increase the resource requirement considerably. And some things need to be iterated, to take advantage of learning from your past experiments. After all, there's no point to experimentation if it doesn't have the chance to influence your future behavior. Along those same lines, we also learn a lot through the experience of actually deploying a new process node in production and running large volumes. That can teach us things that lab experiments never will but which may be crucial to get the next generation to yield at viable levels. If we skip generations, we skip opportunities for learning through volume manufacturing. About every 2-3 generations we make some very significant change (s) to the technology, and if we don't learn how to overcome all of each one's challenges in manufacturing, the next generation could turn into a disaster as those challenges get magnified.

article: Matter (in the everyday sense) is made of molecules, which are made of atoms, which are made of particles: protons, neutrons and electrons. That seemed to be the whole story, and that the component particles of atoms were "fundamental" - they weren't made of anything else, they were just kind of themselves. But then we found out that protons and neutrons are actually made of smaller particles, which are called "quarks." Quarks have some interesting properties. It turns out that quarks have six different "flavors" just intrinsically different varieties. There are only a handful of stable combinations of flavors that will last when they clump together. Other combos break down quickly or never form at all. And most importantly and weirdly, they can't be separated - they can only exist in these combos. Particles made of combinations of quarks are called, as a family, "hadrons." The protons and neutrons we know so well from our daily lives are the most stable combination of quarks, which are made of just two flavors called "up" and "down" quarks. These are also the most stable flavors of quarks - other flavors quickly decay into up and downs. But there are also more exotic combinations of quarks that show up as relatively short-lived particles in cosmic rays and stuff. These can involve combinations of the other four flavors of quark: "strange," "charm," "bottom," and "top." Quarks and hadrons have a lot of other interesting properties and important roles in particle physics. But to everyday human experience, the combos of up and down quarks that we know as protons and neutrons are the biggest part of the picture.','The bartender on Star Trek: Deep Space Nine.','Related: Please explain how a quark and a neutrino are related, if at all.

article: The rule about "no metal in the microwave" is actually one that exists more for the sake of simplicity. It isn't a hard and fast rule of science. There are times when it's okay to have metal in the microwave. Metals reflect most of the microwave energy, which is why the microwave oven itself is made of metal to keep the radiation inside the microwave oven. A metal bowl, in general, is okay to put in the microwave, provided that it's completely smooth and doesn't ever touch the walls of the microwave. It just reflects radiation around in the oven, but doesn't have any sharp prongs to create electrical arcs with. Food products like Hot Pockets have metallic cages that can be used to reflect microwave radiation in a certain way that cooks the food in a desirable way. Whatever metal items come inside the microwave are either designed in a way that won't create arcs, or perhaps, they're made of metal alloys that don't interact much with the radiation. Such alloys do exist.','A lot of microwaveable food comes with some sort of metallic heating shroud in it to help cook better. Then danger is when you put something in that has the right shape and topography to be able to arc. If you put a spoon in the microwave, your microwave will be ok, and the spoon will heat. If you put a fork in, you will get arc between the tines. Those sparks arcing around are what can be harmful to the microwave.', "The top comments are correct, but they don't mention this very simple rule of thumb: sharp angles more likely to spark. In general, anything metal with sharp angles (fork, aluminum foil, etc) is probably a bad idea to microwave. Smooth metal, not so much.

article: Most animal models of cancer use mice without an immune system, and they just inject some cancer cells from a flask into the mouse. Different cancer cells sometimes spread to different parts of the body (e.g. Lung cancer cells spreading to the lungs) and some just form a tumour at the site of injection. Other animal models can use a chemical that causes cancer to induce tumours. Source- PhD student in a cancer research lab Edit- because the mice don't have an immune system, they don't try to get rid of the cancer, because those cells will be foreign to the mouse, the same as bacterial cells that our immune system can attack,Tumor cells are grown in a dish and injected into the rodent. Different types of tumors grow in different injection sites (and grow better in certain places or in specific strains of animals etc). For example, breast cancer cells can grow into a tumor in several places but tend to grow well in the mammary fat pad of female rodents. You can also model metastases by injecting your tumor cells intravenously- they will hit the lungs on their way around, and will settlegrow there.','One method is implanting tissue directly from a patient. Once a patient signs a consent form, a portion of the tumor is brought to the research lab. Immune-compromised micerats are knocked out using anesthetic, an incision is made, and a small piece of the tumor is implanted in the animal just under the skin. When it grows to a large enough size, the tumor is extracted, spilt into many pieces, and implanted in many more mice (or frozen for later use, or collected for analysis, etc.). This is repeated to maintain stocks of mice with the desired tumor type, some of which are then used for studies. Source: do this for a living.','Besides injection of cells, there are genetic models. For breast cancer, there are a couple different extremely well known lines of mice that are extremely predisposed to tumors. For liver cancer, there is a chemical you can inject into baby mice that predisposes them to tumors later in life.','I did some research on melanoma using mice this summer, I can help answer this! My specific project was actually perfecting the method of giving mice cancer to use them as models for cancer treatments. Basically, we order cancer cells from a company that has made a consistent, pure cell line. We feed the cells a nutrient-rich cell food and let them multiply on a plate, then inject the cells right into the mouse and let them do their cancer thing. For our purposes, we injected the mice in the ear since it has a nice supply of blood and the mice couldn't mess with the growing tumors too much (they tend to scratchgnaw at them because tumors smell weird to mice). You can also use a "seed" or "donor" mouse, where you do the same process as above, let the tumor get freakin' huge, euthanize the mouse, cut out the tumor, then mash it into a tumor smoothie and inject THAT into another mouse. This supposedly works better as the cells are adapted to living mice already, but don't quote me on that. Since our project was about measuring immune responses, our mice had fully functioning immune systems. This means that half the time the mice actually resisted the cancer, which was a bummer for our study but good for the mice I guess lol.','They breed rats that have genetic mutations. The other way is to expose them to chemicals and radiations that cause mutations at an early age.', "There are a variety of methods, and it all depends on the cancer and what you're researching which method is utilized. If you're trying to prevent cancer, or see how something interacts with cancerous progenitors, you might use a gene mutation that's known to promote cancerous tumor growth, or expose the group to a carcinogen, and then do a variety of things to see which treatment limits growth or occurrence the most. You can also implant tumors or cancerous cells, which others here have described. You can also do a variety of the above, like irradiate them, expose them to cigarette smoke, and then stress them, and compare rates of growth to a null group, etc.," "I'm a lab student and had to do a research with tisseu from lab rats with cancer. article: A common answer is the spinning wheels act as gyroscopes effectively increasing inertia so a standing object resists falling over (or even starting to tip). That's not the whole story. The geometry of bicycles and motorcycles means that leaning them causes them to steer. Gyroscope effects are sometimes mentioned here too, but it has a lot to do with the shape of the tire. The edge is shorter, and therefore moving slower, than the center of the tire. When leaned, the center wants to cover more ground and "catch up" with the side of the tire. This causes the bike to turn. The turning of the bike makes it straighten up, due to a moving object's tendency to keep moving in a straight line (when turning, it leans to the outside of the curve). Once it straightens up, it stops turning. So you might notice a small deviation from a straight line but it's not going to continue turning. The correction is self-limiting and when you're moving these "corrections" are so quick and constant it just feels like a force or natural tendency for the bike to stay upright.','Minute Physics did a video about it. [Here it is] (URL0). tl;ds: In short a normal bicycle is stable thanks to a combination of: - the front wheel touching the ground behind a backwards tilted steering axis, - the center of mass of the front wheel and handlebars being located in front of the steering axis, - and the gyroscopic precession of the front wheel.', "The kind of sad answer is that we don't really know for sure. The gyroscopic effect is a common answer, but tests have been done to try and cancel out the gyroscopic effect of bikes and they are still fairly self-correcting. And the geometry is mentioned, but people have made very strangely shaped bikes that we can still make work like bikes with relative ease. It seems that each of the working theories on how bicyclesmotorcycles stay up has something to do with it, but there's still some mystery there.,A moving object will not fall over. Most of the inertia in a moving bike is going in the direction which it is moving. On a stationary bike, there is no inertia so a slight force in one direction will knock it down.','The wheels have mass, and with that moment of inertia. The ideal state of anarcho-capitalism is one where all actors follow every agreement without outside interference, because game theory dictates that lying once will cause a negative return in the long run. If all humans were totally rational, this might be able to work, and it could be effectively anarchy, defined as a lack of a centralized government or need of one. Under this, all people would work as hard as they could for their own benefit, and as they know everything and are totally rational, every agreement would be upheld and the free market would run everything at maximum efficency. There would need to be a centralized government to prevent excessive air pollution, for example, as air belongs to everyone and therefore is almost impossible to protect by anyone. article: History is full of shifting alliances. The US and the Russians were allies in WWII, against the Germans. Today the US and the Germans are allies and the Russians are the adversaries. Here are some pretty arbitrary bins: BFF the five eyes US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand Defense Buddies NATO countries, Israel Economic Buddies South Korea, Japan, Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, India Diplomatic Buddies everybody else Frenemies Russia and China Not enough government to suit the US Iraq, Afghanistan, Yemen, Somalia, SudanSouth Sudan, Libya, Nigeria Axis of Evil Iran, Cuba and North Korea (though Cuba was becoming a frenemy under the Obama administration) ','Most of our allies are described by [NATO membership] (URL0). NATO was created as a direct opposition to Soviet expansion, and the allies we recruited to join NATO were countries that were more or less afraid of an eventual Soviet take-over of their country, or were willing to help us even if they were not directly threatened. Those partnerships go back eons. We are allies with France because of our past history of hating the British - them for historical reasons going back centuries, and us for that whole "war of independence" thing. France helped us fight that war, and we probably would not have won our independence without them. Great Britain and the US have a shared history of being a part of Great Britain. Despite the relatively short period of hating the British, we both realized that we have so much in common, linguistically, culturally.... So we became close friends and allies again. Then there was the first World War which saw countries allying for political and economic reasons, then again in WWII when alliances were formed for mostly ideological reasons (fascist governments allying against everyone else). After WWII, the US made it a policy to rebuild the losing countries, partly in response to the growing Soviet threat, but also because we saw what happened after WWI: Germany was devastated financially and it created a space for Hitler's rise to power. We figured if we can build the countries back up they'll be more stable and, hey, we'll get some allies out of it. There's also the [UN membership] (URL1), which are "allies." Our "alliance" with Russia has been a dodgy thing. We were enemies, then when the wall fell we became "allies" to help them "rebuild..."except we kind of didn't. We kind of gave them terrible advice and kind of purposefully tried to screw them up. Then we became "allies" because the alternative is to be enemies again, so it's like "Let's be friends...wink wink nudge nudge please let's not nuke each other..." Some of the other UN members have been somewhat similar in the past (like China) - let's be "friends" so we're not trying to kill each other. There are a lot of other ways we're "allied" with countries, mostly economic partnerships like the controversial T-TIP. Even where there's no military partnership, we try to work together financially, which it's really an alliance but it's worth mentioning. TL;DR: Recently, from the events of the World Wars and the rise of the Soviet Union, but before that it was the shared history and cultures of Europe.

article: First: What is a fart? A big chunk of 'em is methane, a very light gas that can easily blow away. That's a whole different ballgame there, Sparky.). Well, now that we all know what a fart is, through enlightening definition OR unpleasant personal experience, three things happen to its smell over time. A lot of gas in that fart spreads out to the point that there's not enough of it for us to smell. The gas molecules don't go away, they just float around in the air in an ever-increasing volume until they're too weak for us to detect. And they last until those molecules are processed somehow into other molecules such as they fly into a candleflame and burn. Some components get trapped into fabric. Fart naked on a sofa and that cushion will wear your essence for a while. And if the fart has liquid or oily bits in it, that fart stink can last a long time. But the third reason the smell goes away fairly quickly is that we have a survival trait that only pays attention to "new" stuff, smells included, and we quickly erase the stuff that's been around a bit and recognized. Old stuff is not as threatening as anything new is. If someone farted three minutes ago and we squirt a little bit of wood smoke into the same area, people are going to instantly detect that smoky smell even though the fart's still around. Their brains filter out the fart smell after a while (unless it's overwhelming), just like we filter out kitchen smells when we're cooking but someone from another room still shouts "Hey what smells so good?., "ELI5 answer: The stink floats so far away from itself that you can no longer smell it because it is to thin, but an animal with a stronger nose would still be able to. Its kind of like how a cat can see in darkness that humans cannot: we can't see the light, but there is enough light that the cats can see with it.," "As a note, you can train people to smell 1 part per billion or smaller, so dilution isn't the only reason smells go away.,Do the molecules that make up an odor actually break down? article: The speed of light is often assumed to be how fast that light moves, much as we might view a Formula 1 race car. This isn't actually accurate though. A better way to look at it is that the speed of light is simply the speed at which an object moves that has no mass. This is why it cannot be achieved through any conventional means at this time. You will always have mass, therefore you will never reach the speed of light. You will approach it, but you'll never get there because you will never shed all of your mass. Having said that, with infinite fuel you will have infinite mass and this ensures that your top speed is less than the speed of light. Where it actually falls is meaningless because to run the numbers you would need values for your total mass, which would be infinite.," "You could get as close to the speed of light as you want. Never reach it, but as close as you ever wish. Being manned or unmanned doesn't really matter that much other than, humans can only tolerate certain amount of acceleration. It's measured in acceleration Earth's gravity does. Standing on Earth subjects you to 1g of acceleration. Humans die somewhere between 5g and 15g depending on some variables, but basically, because humans only live about 100 years, you only have 100 years of max 15g of acceleration that you can do (actually it's much less, but that's beside the point), which only gets you limited amount of acceleration. For other cargo, you could theoretically accelerate them without really caring about the cargo wellbeing as much, so you could accelerate more, and spend more time accelerating, so you don't have similar extra limit to the speed you can achieve.,From a physics perspective, it's the speed of light. You can get as close as you like, but not reach or exceed it because of the shape of the 4-dimensional spacetime Universe we live in. From an engineering perspective (presuming "we" is people) you can't go nearly as fast as that, manned or unmanned. Space isn't empty enough to go that fast. There is an atom every meter or so, and slamming into an atom at 50 the speed of light is super dangerous. Hitting one faster is even more dangerous. With the physics we have today, 10 of C is an extravagantly generous upper speed. The fastest actual spacecraft is New Horizons at 16.26 kmsec (0.0054 of C).', "Assuming I understand your question, you're asking what would happen if a ship had an infinite amount of fuel? Well given an infinite amount of time, it would approach the speed of light as closely as you could imagine.," "Lots of the answers here provide good answers for why you can never really reach the speed of light completely (although you can get so close its easiest just to say max speed light speed). However almost nobodys mentioned time dilation. I'm not sure theres an easy way to explain it at an ELI5 level (probably requires a more complete understanding of relativistic physics than I possess, but I can give you rough numbers. This also means theres a huge difference between manned and unmanned ships. Under constant acceleration, you hit very high speeds very, very fast. Accelerating at a mere 1g (not hard on a human passenger - if anything it'd probably be relatively comfortable) you would reach lightspeed in about a year. At this point, travelling at lightspeed (again, technically more like 99.9 or whatever), time dilation kicks in heavily. You could, from the point of view of somebody on board the ship, travel the diameter of the galaxy in 12 years. That's a pretty casual time period - you could visit basically anywhere in the entire galaxy in a less than 24 year journey time (you have to decelerate for quite a long time to slow down to a non insane speed to actually do anything more than a quick flyby). From the point of view of somebody chilling on earth however, approximately 110,000 years would have passed (for 12 years at near lightspeed). Humanity would most likely have ceased to exist, at least in any form you understand over the course of your 12 year trip. You could reach andromeda if you wished, easily within the lifespan of the humans on board. Of course, this means the universe would have aged more or less a billion years around you as you flew. But it does mean theres a big difference between manned and unmanned missions. An unmanned mission would experience the same effect - robot probe 1101 would experience not many years having passed, but its a robot so it doesn't matter much. As a squishy, temporally limited human however, it would actually allow you to explore unimaginably distant places within your lifespan (and within a short lifespan for ship-board components) - running an ark style starship to another planet is a long stretch if systems have to last for 110,000 years, not so much if they only have to last 12. Big issue in this of course, is that constant acceleration is really hard. But given unlimited fuel, its not the limiting factor - only lightspeed and local-observer time perception is.,There is a neat different way to ask the question, if you frame it in "what is the max speed to GET SOMEWHERE." Due to time and space dilation when you get close to light speed, you will age slower than the universe around you, and everything ahead of you will squish closer to you than before. Therefore, even though you can't reach the speed of light, you will continually reach far-away places faster, as you approach the speed of light. The trick is that only you will be able to tell that you are getting there faster; any observer will see you travelling at nearly the speed of light, as expected.', "There is no max speed. You would get increasingly closer to the speed of light but you would never reach it. So you would keep going faster and faster, but the increase in speed would get smaller and smaller. For example: After 1 second, you're going 99 the speed of light. After 2 seconds, you're going 99.9 the speed of light. After 3 seconds, you're going 99.99 the speed of light. Etc.," "You could accelerate forever. Relative to other objects you would never observe yourself exceeding the speed of light, but you would also never reach a limit to the acceleration you could provide. Well, with some caveats. Eventually the universe would essentially become a bath of hard radiation and destroy you. But that's a problematic condition, not an actual physical limitation on your acceleration.,In theory if you had an infinite fuel source you could reach basically the speed of light, manned or unmanned. Currently no feasible fuel source for that exists. The main issue would be that if you hit a hydrogen atom floating in space while going that speed it would be like being shot with a shotgun. So you would probably die.

It could be obvious that he did it but if the lawyer can show how it was even remotely possible that someone else did it then the jury has to give him the benefit of the doubt. If he's good he'll take the remotest fact and stretch it into a reasonable doubt. They also work to get evidence thrown out. That was a lot of what happened with OJ, a lot of the best evidence that we saw on tv was never shown to the jury. I saw a special where they interviewed some members of the OJ jury a few years after the trial and they were pissed about the evidence they didn't get to see. They all said if they had seen some of those things the verdict might have been different. A good lawyer can find technicalities that can rule even some of the most damning evidence thrown out. The jury is only allowed to base their decision on what they see in the court room. The prosecutor must convince the jury that the guy did it and it is impossible that any one else could have. Any little bit of doubt, no matter how small, and the jury is not supposed to convict someone.,There must be admissible evidence which is sufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The courts don't allow just any sort of innuendo or speculation to be presented to jurors. It may be "obvious" to people watching television that someone is guilty, but juries don't get the same information.
