article: A big part of what they do is deciding what NOT to decide on. Tens of thousands of cases are submitted to the supreme court every year, but they only have the time to decide on a handful. Many that are submitted have already been decided on, and the justices generally know they're not going to change their minds this time. Others haven't been presented in a way that would set enough of a precedent for the issue. It takes time to review each submittal to the supreme court and decide if it's worth pursuing. Then they take the shortlist and review it even deeper before deciding which cases to actually hear in the next season.,What the justices do on a day to day basis depends on what part of the term they are in and what is on the court calendar. In general, a few main things occupy their time: DECIDING WHAT CASES TO TAKE. 7,000-8,000 of cases get appeals to the Supreme Court every year, but they can only take about 80 each year (plus or minus). They want to make sure they take the most important and interesting cases. Generally, the initial research on what might make for good cases is done by individual justice's "law clerks." Each judge has one or more law clerks, who are usually the best recent graduates from the best law schools. Among other things, the clerks help them research potential cases and brief the justices on what they are about. Then the justices vote on whether to take cases behind closed doors. HEARING CASES LISTENING TO ORAL ARGUMENT. The Supreme Court has a number of days on calendar where they actually listen to their parties argue their case. This happens for a few hours a day, a few days a week. Attorneys try to argue their case while the justices hammer them with questions. DISCUSSING CASES. Depending on the case and calendar, some time will be spent behind close doors discussing the merits of the cases with the other justices, trying to determine how the case should be resolved and whether the court can reach a majority decision. RESEARCHING AND WRITING OPINIONS. The job of the Supreme Court is to decide cases, and they decide cases by writing "opinions." If a majority of the justices can decide how a case should be resolved, the most senior member in that majority usually assigns who should write the opinion. At that point, a lot of the initial research is done by law clerks, and sometimes even some of the writing, although this depends on the justice. Then the justice circulates a draft opinion, gets feedback, and revises it. In the meantime, the other judges in the minority may write concurring or dissenting opinions which are also circulated and edited. This goes back and forth for a while until everything is polished and the decision is ready to be published. READING OPINIONS CEREMONIAL MISCELLANEOUS. Justices also spend some time announcing and reading their opinions after a case is decided. They may have some ceremonial duties (e.g., swearing in elected officials), and various other miscellaneous duties.', "You should watch a few videos on the CSPAN website covering the Supreme Court. They're all online and free. It's the best look inside the court. The also have a Supreme Court week every year when they produce new video.," " Do they sit in some library with stacks of old books, looking up various laws relevant to their current cases, or do other people working for them do that and make reports? Each Justice has between 1 and 4 [law clerks] (URL1). The law clerks are typically new lawyers, 2 years after graduating (the first year after graduating is typically spent at the Court of Appeals). Law clerk for a Supreme Court justice is one of the most prestigious positions for a new law school graduate, typically going to only people who graduated near the top of their class at a very prestigious law school. (I knew a guy who was a student at Columbia Law School (4 in the nation) who transferred to Yale Law School (1 in the nation) just for the better chance of getting a Supreme Court clerkship.) Because it's such a prestigious position, it can be the beginning of a storied legal career. Sen. Ted Cruz was once a Supreme Court law clerk to CJ Rehnquist, as was current CJ Roberts. Justice Kagan was a clerk for Justice Marshall. Justice Breyer was a clerk for Justice Goldberg. (The Justices seem to have patterns of hiring. Obviously, lots of Yale, Harvard, and Stanford grads for every justice. But Scalia had a thing for Chicago grads, Ginsburg has a thing for Columbia grads, Sotamayor likes NYU grads, and Thomas and Kennedy seem to like Virginia grads.) article: Your cable box does not "stream" anything at all. It works on completely different principles. Television is an example of synchronous, circuit-switched communication. Signals (which may or may not be digital; they're usually not) are coming at you all the time at a constant rate. In the case of television, the signals are multiplexed based on fundamental frequency ... which is just a fancy way of saying you get every signal all the time, coming in at that same constant rate always. Your equipment chooses which one to "listen" to. The Internet is an asynchronous, packet-switched communications system. Your equipment only ever receives a single signal at any given time. In order to fit multiple distinct signals down the pipe, each one is broken down into chunks and fed to you chunk-by-chunk. You are not guaranteed to get those chunks at a constant rate; in fact, you're all but guaranteed not to. In order to "convert" from that chunk-by-chunk, asynchronous, digital signal to a continuous, synchronous, analog signal, your equipment has to stash away a bunch of chunks in anticipation of future chunks being delayed. Under the best circumstances, your equipment stores up a sufficiently large reserve of chunks that it never stalls waiting for the next chunk, though they come completely irregularly and unpredictably. But it's often the case that it doesn't work out that way. Or put more simply, the Internet does not deliver synchronous signals because it was never designed to deliver synchronous signals. For a couple decades now, computer nerds have been trying to squeeze the square peg of synchronous broadcast into the round hole of asynchronous packet-switching. It fundamentally doesn't work, though people do get closer from time to time.

article: It probably sounds worse than it really is for the speakers. There are a few types of distortion in audio but when it comes to loud volumes causing distortion, that's called clipping. In the audio electrical circuit, there is "clean headroom" up to a certain volume. Let's say the input audio is 2 volts AC peak to peak. The amplifier circuit has up to 10 V peak to peak of clean headroom. If you turn up the gain (via the volume knob) to a 10x gain, it will clip causing distortion. Even though the input was 2V and the gain was 10x, the output will only be slightly higher than 10 V, (probably a bit below 11 V) but it will sound very distorted. As long as the cell phone manufacturer paired a speaker that can handle the maximum output of the integrated amplifier, your cell phone speaker will be fine. The cell phone manufacturer may have even intentionally designed clipping to limit the output. In other amplifier speaker setups like guitars and home stereo, that is where it can be a problem. Many things need to be considered for pairing a speaker and amplifier. Home hi-fi, PA setups, and guitarbass amps all have very high clean headroom (lots of volts of potential gain) so the total amplification can be very high and clipping is usually not intentionally used to limit the output (except for guitar some guitar amps settings and cheap home stereos). In addition to the voltage amplifier that multiplies the voltage, they have large power amplifiers that increase the current output to drive the large speakers. Which is a very different design from the cell phones because they have a buffer circuit drive the speaker rather than a power amplifier. the buffer just matches the impedence to the little speaker but doesn't really increase the wattage very much because it's such a small speaker. With some amplifiers the output goes through a transformer. If the speaker and transformer do not have matched impedences, the transformer can burn out and damage the rest of the amplifier. If the speakers cannot handle the total output in watts of the amplifier, the speakers coil can burnout. In vintage speakers, the cone could rip. Also if a bass guitar amp is used on a vintage or cheap guitar speaker cabinet, the cone could rip. In modern (past 20 years or so) decent quality speakers, the speakers will be fine but the sound would distort and sound farty. Make sure the speakers have the same impedence as needed by the amplifier. Make sure the wattage of the speakers exceeds the wattage of the amplifier. Speakers are often advertised with its peak ratings. You need to match the RMS wattages of the speaker and amp. Don't use peak watts when pairing speakers with an amp. For good sound, make sure you use the right type of speaker with the amplifier. Use hi-fi speakers with hi-fi amps. Use guitar speakers for guitar amps. Use similar wattage ratings: if it's a 100W amp, use a 100W speaker. If possible, buy a matched set of speakers and amps of the same brand and series. The manufacturer probably matched the amp and speakers for a reason.

article: Craters on the Earth just get eroded away from wind, water, life, etc but on the moon they are permanent, only getting covered up by dust from other impacts.','There are multiple reasons. One is the Moon has no atmosphere for anything to burn up in. No atmosphere also means no weather to erode the surface via wind and rain. Anything that happens on the Moon will stay that way unless an external force changes it. This means a crater on the moon that happened millions of years ago will still be around like it just happened (unless another meteor hits in the same spot). Second is that the Moon is not geologically active like the Earth is. Land on Earth floats on a molten area around the core causing the surface to change over time (this is why we have mountains and cliffs and such). Impact sites on Earth can effectively be erased because of this.', " I get that many strikes would get burned up in the atmosphere, but the Moon is covered in craters. You just answered your own question. It doesn't take a large meteor to leave a large crater. Many of the meteors that left those craters on the moon would have been small enough to burn up in Earth's atmosphere. Space is a turbulent place, especially when the gravity from the sun and its surrounding planets gets involved. Meteors come our way frequently, but most of them simply burn up and that's that. No one pays them any mind (well, some people do) because they aren't large enough to remain intact after hitting our atmosphere. Since the moon doesn't have the luxury of an atmosphere, each and every meteor makes it to the surface no matter how big, and as a result, it's covered in craters. Also, it's worth pointing out that the craters on the moon are the result of billions of years of bombardment. After a while, that begins to add up.," "There are two reasons. The first is, as you note, the Earth has an atmosphere. A lot of the meteors that might strike the earth burn up on the way down, and even those that don't burn up entirely have a lot of their energy bled off through friction with the air, so the craters they create are smaller. The second is that the Earth has a lot more going on, from oceans full of water to tectonic plates moving around to all manner of plant and animal life constantly modifying the surface of the Earth. As a result, a crater on the Earth lasts a lot less time than an equivalently-sized crater on the moon. Some of them get eroded away by water (or just filled with water and look like a lake rather than a crater), some of them get destroyed when volcanos erupt, some of them are worn down by the wind, some of them are covered dirt and then by trees, etc. None of that happens on the moon, so a lot more of them are visible today.,Just to tack on to what the others have said. When astronomers look around the solar system at other moons.... The absence of hugely cratered surface is evidence of a geologically active world.

article: Light scatters off interfaces. The more interfaces there are, the more scattering there can be. Clothes and hair consists of many fibres (intertwined together, hopefully only in the former case). All these fibres have a fibreair interface where light can scatter. Because there are many of these interfaces, a lot of light is scattered - mostly back towards your eye. When things get wet, water gets in where air used to be - so instead of fibreair interfaces, you get fibrewater interfaces. It turns out that light doesn't scatter as much when it is fibre and water (advanced level: how much light scatters back depends on the difference in [indices of refraction] (URL1), and because the difference is much smaller between fibre and water than fibre and air, there is less scattering). This cuts down on the total amount of light that scatters back to your eye. Because what we perceive as brightness is due to amount of light reaching your eyes, less light coming back to your eyes means the object seems darker. It is also because less light gets scattered that more light makes it through the material. This means that a wet spot on a wet T-shirt would look brighter if you hold it up against a light source. This is also the governing principle behind why T-shirts can become see-through when wet. In the future, you can also [search past threads] (URL0), as this has been answered a number of times.

article: The main difference between the effects of an atomic bomb detonated in space and that on the ground are not related to gravity, but are related to the fact that the bomb is going off without an atmosphere (air) around it. When a bomb goes off, a lot of the energy is released as thermal and ionizing radiation (heat radiation and nuclear radiation). In an atmosphere (that is, relatively near the surface of the Earth or on it), a good amount of that energy is immediately absorbed into a shell of air surrounding the bomb. This super hot shell of air then bursts out, causing the well-known pressure (blast) effects of the bomb - the stuff that knocks down houses and smashes everything. In the absence of an atmosphere, the heat and nuclear radiation are not as dissipated, and the blast pressure is much more muted. As a result, a nuclear weapon detonated in space is mostly heat and nuclear radiation, and both of those effects go further than they would on Earth, because they are not being absorbed by any atmosphere. The other main difference is that the electromagnetic pulse effect of the bomb, which is relatively limited at near-surface altitudes, can go much, much further and be much more powerful. This can disable satellites and even certain types of electrical circuits on Earth, over a very wide area. As with all high airbursts, there would be no local nuclear fallout. The radiation, however, can linger in space for a long time, which has implications for satellites and radio communications. There would be no mushroom cloud, which is a function of the fireball being in an atmosphere as well. (The fireball is hot and less dense than the atmosphere, so it rises. The movement of a less dense substance through a dense one produces the familiar mushroom-cloud appearance.) Gravity has no effect on allowing the blast to expand or compressing it. It is too weak a force to affect that. It is not possible to make a black hole from a nuclear explosion; black holes are formed by putting lots of matter into one place. A nuclear explosion does not do anything like this.

For example, if experiments show that adding an hour per week of homework increase IQ by an average of 5 points that will likely carry over to other groups of students. On an individual level it's much less useful. 80 vs 130 is a big difference so you're likely to see differences in aptitude but you might not. If the kid with the 80 IQ is an ESL student their result could be downward biased. If the kid with the 130 IQ had parents who coached them on how to take IQ tests (as my parents did) that score is likely to be biased upward. As you also noticed, hard work makes a huge difference. If the kid with the 80 IQ is busy practicing writing while the kid with the 130 IQ is busy minmaxing his Pokemon collection there's a good chance that the kid with the higher IQ could end up looking like the slow one at the end of the year.," "The best analogy I've read is to engine displacement. The students with higher IQ might pick something up more quickly but might also be more likely to be distracted when the class moves at a pace all the students can keep up with. article: So in the early days of cell phones, the answer was YES. That's because the earliest cell phones were analog, just like land lines. As long as you had reasonably good reception without a lot of static or other noise, you could connect a cell phone to a fax machine and it would work. However, for more than a decade now all cell phones have been using exclusively digital transmission. When you speak into your phone, your phone converts that audio into digital bits, compresses it heavily to take as little space as possible, and then transmits the bits to the cell phone tower. The problem is with that digital compression. Digital compression of audio was designed to preserve as much clarity as possible for the human ear, and a big piece of that is throwing away frequencies that humans can't hear. This general field of study is called psychoacoustics. When a fax machine (or any modem) sends a signal over a telephone line, it assumes that all frequencies within a certain range will be transmitted equally well. It uses sounds of different frequencies to encode the different signals it wants to send. When you take the sounds from a fax machine or modem and apply digital voice compression on them, it throws away some of the frequencies that were critical to encoding the message!," "could I theoretically hook the audio directly into the fax machine to receive it? No. That wouldn't work as your fax machine would be trying to send things back to the other one as well, and would expect responses to that. Fax is bidirectional communication and on your cell you only have one side. Otherwise though it would be possible technically to have an app that will take the sound of the fax and turn it into an image. It would not however be simple as demodulating the signal (and there are quite a few different ones it can be) and re-assembling the picture from the digital stream you now have, would take a while. article: The browser doesn't decide much at all, in this case. It makes requests to a server or servers. They start to provide the data based on their capability, loading, and the priority that they give to those particular requests. As those bitstreams make their way to you, they can encounter network congestion along the way, so some may make it to you more quickly than others. The sending of the information is somewhat interactive. The streams of data are broken up into packets, which are aggregated with other packets at multiple levels for transmission along the internet, and then broken up as they get close to their destination. And the server doesn't necessarily just blast out all of the packets at once, without even knowing that they are being received correctly...that would be inefficient. The packets that arrive quickly (either because the server is providing them more rapidly, or because of network conditions) will then cause your computer to respond "OK, got that chunk, please send some more." The browser is generally going to be limited by your network bandwidth or some other bottleneck, so it simply sits back and says the networking equivalent of "FEED ME" until it has gotten everything it requested. If you want to understand how things like this work in detail, you might want to read up on the [Media Access Control (MAC) ] (URL0) and [Logical Link Control] (URL1) layers of the 7-layer OSI networking model. Even if you don't fully understand them at first (and you won't), you'll start to get a better idea about how networking really works.

article: An average European worker tends to produce more value in a given hour of work than the average worker in an Asian country. Think of the economy as a collection of row boats. Pairs of "workers" sitting in each row boat are rowing in opposite directions and the boats stay more or less stationary. Each worker is fighting for his employer's share of wealth. Those opposing sides might be two competitors but could also be a government bureaucrat vs. a corporate bureaucrat. Now, if one side rows harder the other side also has to row harder in order to win back their slice of the pie. In Europe, the government is more interventionist than in Asia (there are stricter labor laws) and mandates that both sides should row a little less hard. article: You might also take a look at MariaDB, SQLite and Oracle to complete your list of relational databases. The main differences is performance features, cost and footprint. Oracle and MsSQL is the most expensive, have a high minimum resource use but have a lot of performance features. The other databases on the list will for instance have problems using multiple cores to improve speed. PostgreSQL is the most enterprise open source database and have quite a big list of features and good performance. It is also the database that will allow the most customization. It is free but there are companies that provide licensed third party support if you want. MySQL and MariaDB are smaller open source databases that were recently the same project so they share a lot of the same features. It does not have the same rich feature set as the more enterprise database engines but does have a much lower footprint and is a good compromise for medium size applications. MySQL does have a licensed option with a bit more features but in general they are both open source and free to use. SQLite is as the name suggest a very light weight database engine. It is designed to easily fit inside other applications, in cell phones or other embedded devices. However this does mean that it have a lot of limitations and does not have good performance. It is also open source and free to use. So they all have different features and is made for different things. If you have millions of simultaneous users and have to store critical data then you should consider paying for MsSQL or Oracle. However if the data is not as critical and does not need that much performance then PostgreSQL is the right tool for the job. For smaller applications where the idle resource requirements is important MariaDB is likely the best tool. But if you just need to store a few values and query them from time to time then SQLite is the best option.

In HTML4, if you wanted a video, you had to reach for Flash or Silverlight and embed the video in a site with code (think about the old cut-and-paste stuff to embed content that YouTube would provide). In HTML5, there are audio and video elements integrated into the language - no external plugins required. There's drag-and-drop capability (like how you can drag and drop a file into SkyDrive in your browser, or the way gmail has integrated drag-and-drop), so there's more interaction programmed in. For example, you could write something in Office365 or GoogleDocs even with no internet connection and then it would sync the next time you're online.,This is a bit of a complex question so I'll answer it as best I can. New "semantic" tags HTML5 is the next step in creating a more "semantic web," meaning that browsers can more easily tell what format certain data is in. In the past, web pages have been structured using something called "divs" (which, in code is the div tag). In order to differentiate them, most coders use an attribute within the div tag, known as "id" or "class." This is like giving a label to that div so it's known by a specific name or group. (For example: if I have a div that will serve as the header of my page, I might use the tag div id"header" .) This is all fine and well, but when a browser reads this code, it can't understand that this specific div is meant to be the header of the page. It just knows that it's called "header." In HTML5, there is actually a tag now called header . This adds "semantic value," or meaning, to the tag itself, meaning that it's easier for a browser that reads the code to know that this section is the header of a page. So, why is that important? It's for the sake of search engines like Google, who can filter through certain parts of a page when you're looking for something and improve the quality and the accuracy of your search results, making it easier for you to find what you're looking for. This same concept applies to a lot of other elements of the page. Instead of using a generic object tag that could be one of many things (images, audio, video, Flash, etc.), you can now use semantic tags called video or audio . So, instead of the browser reading the code and saying "okay, this is an object, now what type is it?," it will say "okay, this is clearly a video." The canvas tag Think about all of the fancy animations and such that Flash webpages are able to do. The canvas tag will allow web designersdevelopers to achieve many of those same effects using just HTML and JavaScript code (JavaScript being another powerful web language that works with HTML to create complex actions and applications) instead of needing to use Flash, which can be slow to load and bandwidth-heavy. Why is this a good thing? It simplifies the process of designing rich graphics and interactive elements without needing to learn and resort to a third-party technology like Flash. It's also more portable and scalable to mobile browsing, whereas Flash has had well-documented problems making the jump to smartphones. Application caching Ever been doing something on a webpage (like using an application or filling out a form) and your internet connection went out, so you lose your data and can't finish what you were doing? HTML5 solves that problem by using what's called "application caching." Basically, when the browser reads the code and comes across a tag that looks like this: html manifest"filename.manifest" .... it will read the manifest file to figure out what files a specific webapp needs to run. It will then download them and store them on your computer so that if you need to use the webapp offline, it will still function. Why is this a good thing? Obviously, it allows for a lot more flexibility in terms of how webapps are used. If you're on the go and you can't get WiFi or 3G coverage, you can still use those webapps to accomplish various things without needing an internet connection. Those are just a couple of reasons, but they're what I'd call the major ones. It's really about helping code writers write cleaner, simpler and less code, while improving HTML's capabilities and organizing data better so it's easier to sort and find. HTML5 is still in development and isn't scheduled to be finalized until around 2022, but many of its abilities are already being implemented into more progressive webpages. The drawback is that browsers don't have full capability to understand everything that HTML5 tries to do, so some of it breaks. When you're designing a webpage, you need to consider "cross-browser compatibility," meaning that you make sure the page will look the same and work the same, no matter what browser or version someone is using. Internet Explorer 6 is notoriously bad for developers because it doesn't support many of the newer features and many people (usually older people or non-computer savvy people) don't understand the importance of upgrading their browser, so web developers will need to cater to the lowest common denominator in many cases. article: In physics, there are lots of things that move in circles or rotate, so it's obviously useful there. It's way more interesting than that, though. Suppose you're on a Ferris wheel. I know how fast the Ferris wheel rotates, and what I'm interested in is knowing what height above the ground you're at at any given point in time. So, since Ferris wheels are circles, we'll study circles. Take a look at [this] (URL1). If you imagine that the circle is the Ferris wheel, y is your height at any given point in time (assume you're at point P). Because I took trigonometry in high school, I know that a mathematical function called the "sine function" is what gives me y. Specifically, sin (th) y, where th is the angle (you can see it labeled in the diagram). So, I know that sin (th) is what tells me how high you are at any given point in time. If I were to plot that on a graph, it would look like [this] (URL2). Like you'd expect, you're going up and down over and over as the Ferris wheel spins, it makes a lot of sense. Before I get too far ahead of myself, I want to remind you where sine comes from. It comes from a circle, it directly involves pi. There is no sine without pi, whenever I use sine, pi pops up. Alright, so when you look at the picture of the sine function, it looks sort of like a wave. It's actually typically called a "sine wave." That is not a coincidence. If we want to describe a wave in physics, we use sine (and cosine, its buddy). Sound waves? Sine. Light? Sine. Electrons? Sine. Literally any wave phenomenon, and I mean any wave phenomenon (other than water waves which are tricky) can be described in terms of sine. Not only that, but they can be described entirely using sine, you don't have to use anything else, ever. It's not just waves, either. Any sort of "oscillatory phenomenon," ie one that repeats itself over and over, we use sine. Pendulum? Sine. AC electricity? Sine. Vibrating string? Sine. Jiggling a slinky? Sine. Pi will rear its head whenever you try to talk about any of those things, as well as a bajillion other scenarios. At its heart, whenever we talk about "something that oscillates," it's the same as talking about your height as you ride a Ferris wheel. edit: [Here] (URL0) is an animation of how travelling around the "Ferris wheel" generates the sine function which I'm totally stealing from a post uDelehal just made.

article: The 18th Amendment was the result of decades of campaigning by temperance groups. While there had been anti-alcohol groups in America basically since the first settlers, a few thing came together in the late 19th and early 20th centuries that gave the temperance movement the momentum it needed. The main factor was the rise of evangelical Christianity, which often preached that drinking was a sin. Also, many middle-class Americans (especially women) saw drinking as a moral failing and associated it with urbanization, immigration, and industrialization. By the early 20th century, temperance groups had become very influential in national politics. They argued that alcohol was the cause of many social problems, such as crime, poverty, and domestic violence. The Anti-Saloon League, which was the most powerful of these groups, succeeded in getting many local and state governments to adopt "dry" laws, which prohibited the sale and consumption of alcohol. This was seen as a way to reduce the power of saloon owners and corrupt politicians who they claimed were in league with them. When World War I began in 1914, the temperance groups took advantage of the patriotic fervor and linked their cause to national defense. They claimed that using grain to make alcohol was unpatriotic because it took food away from the troops. In 1917, President Woodrow Wilson supported the idea of a constitutional amendment to prohibit alcohol, and in 1919, the 18th Amendment was ratified, making the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcohol illegal in the United States.

This header message is followed by a loud, prolonged beep that's designed to get your attention (it works!), which is then followed by an announcer or computerized voice informing you of what's going on. article: Diwali also called Divali, Deepavali or the "festival of lights," is a five-day Hindu festival which starts on Dhanteras, celebrated on the thirteenth lunar day of Krishna paksha (dark fortnight) of the Hindu calendar month Karthick and ends on Bhaiduaj, celebrated on the second lunar day of Shukla paksha of the Hindu calendar month Kartik. Dhanteras usually falls eighteen days after Dussehra. In the Gregorian calendar, Diwali falls between mid-October and mid-November. Diwali is an official holiday in India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Mauritius, Guyana, Trinidad Tobago, Suriname, Malaysia, Singapore and Fiji. For Hindus, Diwali is one of the most important festivals of the year and is celebrated in families by performing traditional activities together in their homes. For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha or nirvana by Mahavira in 527 BC. For Sikhs, Diwali is particularly important because it celebrates the release from prison of the sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, and 52 other princes with him, in 1619. Arya Samajists, celebrate this day as Death Anniversary of Swami Dayanand Saraswati. They also celebrate this day as Shardiya Nav-Shasyeshti. The name "Diwali" or "Divali" is a contraction of deepavali which translates into "row of lamps" Diwali involves the lighting of small clay lamps filled with oil to signify the triumph of good over evil. These lamps are kept on during the night and one's house is cleaned, both done in order to make the goddess Lakshmi feel welcome. Firecrackers are burst because it is believed that it drives away evil spirits. During Diwali, all the celebrants wear new clothes and share sweets and snacks with family members and friends. The festival starts with Dhanteras on which most Indian business communities begin their financial year. The second day of the festival is called the Naraka Chaturdasi. Amavasya, the third day of Diwali, marks the worship of Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth. The fourth day of Diwali is known as Kartika Shudda Padyami. article: Calculating the masses of stars is actually fairly straightforward under certain circumstances, mainly that we can observe something orbiting around those stars. We know from our understanding of gravity and motion how orbits works, and we can predict very well the orbits of things in our solar system, so it's a very solid theory. So if we have something like a planet (or even a 2nd star) orbiting a star, we can make a few straightforward measurements that let us determine the mass of the star fairly accurately. The first measurement is the timing: how long does it take for the planet to make one complete orbit. The second measurement is the orbital speed: how fast the planet is moving (or, equivalently and easier to measure, the star will wobble slightly because of the planet's gravity, so how fast is it wobbling?). This can be measured straightforwardly through Doppler shift measurements on the light coming from the star. So with these two measurements, we can use the equations that describe the orbit, and turn them around. We know the timing and the speed, so we can determine the size of the orbit and how heavy the central star must be. As long as our measurements are accurate (and they can be done very accurately these days), our estimate of the star's mass can be quite accurate as well, within a few percent in many cases. Edit: A lot of people like the say that we can't really know, or that it's'just theory'. But all it is, in many cases, is simple applications of basic laws of physics that we have tested very very thoroughly on Earth. The laws of orbital mechanics are very well understood; we use them every time we launch a satellite.,If you know what its made out of and how much of what its made out of weighs AND you know how big it is then you know the weight!

article: In short, bodily fluids contain something that absorbs most of the energy from UV light, but not all of it, and the leftover is reflected in the visible spectrum - the energy lost, bringing the UV light into the visible range, is converted to heat. The electron will move back down an energy level and that energy will be released, often times as low-energy light that isn't visible, such as infrared. In this case, bodily fluids fluoresce under UV because they absorb some of the energy, but release some of it in the visible range rather than in lower frequencies. In the case of semen, the presence of flavin or choline proteins causes it to light up under UV. For saliva, it's alpha amylase - an enzyme.,Keep in mind that bloodstains do not glow under a blacklight, but bleach used to clean blood does. also, the chemical luminol will attach to blood (specifically the iron) and the luminol will fluoresce. Blood by itself goes black under a blacklight, so some combination of the above is used to look for blood at a scene. So no, not every bodily fluid will glow under a blacklight. Sweat, saliva, urine, and semen will all glow under a blacklight. For saliva in particular, it seems to be enzymes which are the culprits. a amylase has a specific glow colour under a blacklight. article: Anything that isn't at absolute zero emits thermal radiation. The atoms and molecules are jiggling around (that's what temperature means), and when they bump into each other and stuff, photons get emitted. We call those photons "thermal radiation." The hotter the substance is, the higher energy photons it will emit. So, for example, a lightbulb works by running electricity through a filament. The filament gets really hot, so it emits lots of thermal radiation. It's hot enough that the photons have enough energy to be in the visible light spectrum, which is why it makes visible light. Most objects at regular Earth temperatures are much cooler than a lightbulb. At those temperatures, the bulk of the thermal radiation emitted is infrared. You can think about it this way: when you get something really hot, it starts glowing red. Before it reaches that temperature, though, it's emitting radiation with less energy than red light, ie infrared.', "Any wavelength in the Electromagnetic spectrum can transfer heat. If you radiate more heat, you get higher frequencies of electromagnetic radiation. IR radiation is just what's common to the temperatures around what we're used to.

article: Someone creates a story, called a DM. Other someones create characters. The story can either be very planned out, or something that gets made up on the spot or a mix. Sometimes, you can buy a full "story" in a box, and then the DM just runs the story and adds color as the characters play. the game itself is all the rules that allow you to decide what happens in the story, and what the characters are like. This can be everything from a way to decide whether an arrow hits it's target, or how many spells a wizard has, or what the odds are of getting randomly targeted by thieves when traveling between cities. But the DM and the players are free to tweak these if they think it will be more fun.','Dungeons and dragons is a tabletop roleplaying game. Essentially, players take the role of characters and interact in a shared, imagined world. One player acts as the "dungeon master" who facilitates the game by being the one in charge of creating and managing the world, non-player characters, and other things the player characters interact with. This is pretty much how all tabletop role playing games work. The rules described in D D's books lay out a framework for how to resolve actions in the game world. Generally the way actions are resolved in D D is by rolling a 20 sided die (with a bonus applied to indicate how good your character is at performing the action) and attempting to surpass some specific number that indicates the action was successful. If I want my character to swim across some raging river rapids, the dungeon master assigns a difficulty to the action (say, "20," meaning my roll on the 20 sided die plus my character's bonus for swimming must meet or exceed 20 in order for my character to successfully swim across). That's the basics of how the game works, anyway.', "Imagine a collaborative session of writing an episode of a fantasy action-adventure series. The producerdirector comes to the table with the bones of a story - the main guest stars, the basic plot, the goals and challenges and aims that will make up the framework. However, instead of sharing the whole thing with the team, he only shares the introduction to start with - and everyone else gets into character and takes the initiative to drive it along from inside the story. As they go along, the DM keeps the reins, introduces scenarios and characters relevant to the plot, vetoes anything too silly OP out of character, to keep the story more or less on course. There can be formal rules and stats (equivalent to a'show bible to determine what characters can and can't get away with. A wizard might be mighty, but he can't just fireball his way through an entire army (rinse and repeat for warrioirs, archers, priests, etc); there are tables of figures determining the exact powers and limits thereon that people and monsters have. To prevent conclusions from being foregone, outcomes are often determined by dice rolls - performing a feat of strength successfully would require you to roll a number lower than your'strength' stat, for instance. The DM also enforces limits on what characters would do say put up with, for instance. If you're in a party of goody-two-shoes types and you decide to torture your enemies for information, the others won't be allowed to stand for it. 'Winning', or having the characters reach their stated objective, is not a mandatory goal of the DM. They're meant to be given the opportunity, but it shouldn't be guaranteed by any means.," "In simple terms, it's a story telling game for 2 or more people. article: Aquatic biologist here. I think the real question is "why are open ocean fish so dull"? A great many reef fish are colorful, so are a great many freshwater fish, especially those that aren't "open water" fish. Really, many fish are very colorful or boldly patterned. I think the answer is "because they can be." Open water fish (ocean or freshwater) live in a solid blue environment with nothing to hide behind. They are often (but not always) that classic silvery or flat blue fish color. But fish near reefs (or in small streams) have other options. They have shelter to hide behind if they spot a predator (meaning camouflage isn't as important). That means they can more easily use brilliant colors as social or sexual signals. If they want to be camoflaged, they can use color or pattern as a means to hide rather than being limited by a featureless environment.

article: All the major news outlets are businesses attempting to maximize their profits. All news outlets consider themselves "biased towards the center" but they need to differentiate themselves from their competitors if they want to survive. As the audience changes, the major news outlets need to shift their biases to keep up. Otherwise some other news outlet will steal their audience. Media bias is just a weird topic to me, I don't see why there can't be news outlets that provide real, undramatized news that respect both the right and left so that people can form their opinions for themselves. This is impossible due to the problem of "anchoring." Consider a world where people on the right want the tax rate to be 1 lower and people on the left want the tax rate to be 1 higher. The news outlet reports both sides with equal respect. Then one side decides to play a little trick, and declare that they want the tax rate to change by 90 instead of 1. Now what is the news outlet supposed to do? If they treat this proposal with respect, they are biased towards the radicals. If they don't treat this proposal with respect, they are biased towards the other side. The news outlet has to make a decision on what is and is not reasonable, and that decision will always be considered biased by somebody.', "Actually, the early days of mass journalism (120 years ago or so) were even more biased than today's media. As newspapers consolidated, they found they could attract a bigger audience and make more money by shifting to the center. They also started facing competition from TV and radio, so they cultivated prestige and high journalistic standards as a way to compete. As others have pointed out, it's nearly impossible to completely eliminate bias, so papers like the NYT or the WSJ do have a distinct editorial slant. But they also feature solid researchsourcing, and do their best to keep their reporting and editorial content as separate as possible. Early TV news was somewhat similar. There were high capital and regulatory barriers to become a TV network, so until the late 80s, there were basically only 3. Since they had the same need to attract a large audience across the political spectrum, and had a certain degree of government oversight (under the theory that the frequency bands that they used were a public good, so they had to play by certain rules to have access to them), they copied the newspapers with in-depth reporting, careful attention to sources and accurate facts and so on. The big game-changer was cable (and then the internet). Since cable used private infrastructure instead of public airwaves, they didn't have to play by the same rules, and because the number of channels grew, moving away from the center became a way to differentiate yourself from the other news outlets. Competing for a larger slice of a smaller pie, as it were. Also, with so many channels, sensationalizing your content became a plus that would attract viewers instead of undermining your credibility. Also, with the rise of 247 cable news channels starting with CNN, stations had more time than they could possibly fill merely reporting the news. So editorial content (which by it's nature is guaranteed to be more biased than straight reporting) took over.," "It is impossible to write something without any accusations of bias. Imagine the editor of the local crime desk at a newspaper when a murder occurs. If you include the race of the perpetrator you will receive accusations of bias from one side, and if you omit it you will receive them from others. And that's just one choice of dozens that you'd have to make over the simplest article. Further, the news model changed dramatically when people stopped paying for it. In the past, newspapers supported themselves with classified ad revenue and subscriptions, so they could afford to weather the loss of advertisers and limit their influence on the editorial staff. Now, since every one consumes news for free, the advertisers have much more sway over content.," "Try an exercise for yourself and make a small one paragraph report on some argument two of your friends had or your parents had. article: Both have to do with chemical imbalances in the brain. What you're talking about has a clinical term called "Anhedonia" which is the inability to feel pleasure and is an actual clinical symptom and diagnosis. The big one in depression is the lack of serotonin. Serotonin helps us feel hungry when we are, helps us sleep when we're tired, helps us regulate our mood, and inhibits some pain (Cymbalta is marketed to help with this). If your body knows it's tired and hungry, it's not going to want to do anything until those physiological needs are taken care of (Think Maslow's hierarchy of needs). The other big one is dopamine, which is often regarded as part of the brain's reward system. This is why people with PSA (poly-substance abuse) often seek drugs. It releases dopamine. However with depression dopamine at a reduced level. No reward means no action. One of the biggest thing someone with depression can do is to exercise. Study shows it helps. I'm no expert, but just took a class which covered some of this, but it's really amazing what the brain does, and experts will tell you a lot of what the medical field does, they don't know the mechanism of action, but they just know "it works.,'To be honest, exercise truly does help. That is one thing I would share with others as well','There's no single theory that is accepted for mood disorders. But there are a lot of parts that you can take together to explain it. From a neuropsychological perspective, depression has its effect on two main areas. The first is the area at the forefront of your brain, behind your forehead. The Prefrontal Cortex or PFC. The second is the limbic system, a somewhat deep rooted connected series of structures that sit below your walnut-like hemispheres. The PFC is what makes you who you are. Your personality, motivation, drive and internal goals all come from here. The limbic system is what regulates your emotions. How you feel, what you fear and love, how you recall emotions and emotionally react to everything is based in here. The neuropsych aspect looks at the interplay between these two structures. Think of your mood as being a tug of war between these two players, and the way you are as a person is determined by which brain circuit is more active. Others look at the monoamine hypothesis, which suggests that mood disorders are simply a result of transmitter imbalance in these areas. Which is why drugs are used to effect a change and control the problem. In either case, emotions have an effect on internal motivation. You could argue that most humans, even the most logical ones, do things out of an emotional core or drive. Depression isn't just unhappiness. It's numbness. It's pervasive sadness and a LACK of satisfaction and joy. Most depressed people have a hard time feeling motivated due to this imbalance, and in most cases, the negative mood that comes with it also impacts the motivation and drive of the person suffering. So it becomes a bad cycle, "You're in a bad mood, but you don't want to do anything, so your mood worsens and leaves you more incapacitated." Not everybody reaches this stage. If you look at depression as a spectrum, the key is to get help quickly. If you're slightly more mindful or have recovered from an episode, you can get out of it by doing things to automatically boost your mood. Like the peaceful high from a nice run or exercise, natural endorphins work really well for that. You said that you've been diagnosed with a bipolar mood disorder. So you would had to have had a moment where your mood was pretty high. You might have noticed that you'd have been extremely motivated, productive and even prodigous at your work. It's the same deal. TL;DR The brain circuits that control your emotion experience faulty transmission, and that affects your mood, which also affects your drive and motivation. These brain circuits interact with each other and effectively pull each other down. The same happens in mania, but in the opposite direction. Essentially, it boils down to this: Emotion affects your motivation, and your actions will have an impact on your emotions.', "As I understand it, depression is a loss of interest and a lot of times a loss of drive. Depression can't just be flipped off, obviously, with most psychological problems. As well, the things that used to make you happy (sports, hobbies, meeting and interacting with people) simply don't anymore. The unhappiness partially stems from whatever is causing the depression, be it hormones, brain chemistry, or actual physiological differences, and from the fact that you don't get the joy from the things that used to make you happy. article: We stitch the nerve ends together and let the body heal itself, so basically both your ideas are right. A nerve is made up of several bundles of what we call axons, which are the long, slender projections of nerve cells that transmit signals between the brain or spinal cord and the rest of the body. When a nerve is cut or damaged, the axons can no longer send signals, which can result in loss of sensation, movement, or other functions. To repair a damaged nerve, surgery is often necessary to bring the two cut ends of the nerve back together. This is called nerve repair or nerve suture. The surgeon carefully aligns the nerve ends and stitches them together using tiny sutures or stitches. The nerve then begins to heal itself, and the axons gradually regrow and reconnect with the other side of the nerve. Sometimes, a nerve gap is too big to be repaired through direct suturing. In these cases, a nerve graft may be used. This involves taking a piece of nerve from another part of the body and transplanting it into the gap to bridge the two ends of the damaged nerve. In either case, nerve regeneration is a slow process that may take several months or even years, and the degree of recovery will depend on a variety of factors, including the type and severity of the injury, the age and overall health of the patient, and the success of the surgery and rehabilitation.

In contrast, parallel lights will stay on even if a bulb is removed, as each bulb has its own individual circuit and power source. LED lights are typically wired in parallel, while traditional Christmas lights are often wired in series.

article: Who says they don't? First thing I do as soon as I get home is take them off.,It's easiest to explain this initially by looking at why people of many Asian cultures DO take their shoes off. I can't speak for all Asian cultures, but I've spent a good amount of time in Japan and over there, the floor plays a far more significant part in daily life than it does in the west, despite the increasing modern popularity of western furniture and beds. Traditionally, the Japanese sit directly on the floor, possibly with a cushion, around a low table. This is where you eat, socialise and work. When you sleep, the bedding material is rolled out directly onto the floor, and then put away again the next morning. On that basis, it's clear that having a clean and pleasant floor is extremely important, and as a guest it's culturally significant to take your shoes off as a mark of respect for your host and for their home. Compare that with the west, where we have historically always raised our living space upward. Chairs and dining tables for eating, matresses on bed frames for sleeping; in stark contrast to Asian attitudes it's culturally accepted that the floor is a dirty place, and that it's okay for it to be dirty. So it's not that we don't take our shoes off in the USUK, it's merely that there is no specific culturally mandated rule that we must, and so people are free to make their own house rules based on their personal preference, upbringing, and living situation. Some people mix and match and have intentionally hard-wearing and easy to clean floors downstairs so that it's no problem to keep your shoes on, and then a "no shoes upstairs" rule where it's carpeted. I personally take my shoes off in my house as it has carpet throughout. As a guest, your behaviour is generally expected to conform to that of your host, and whether you may leave your shoes on or not when you visit someone is dependant on what they themselves are doing.','I absolutely do remove my shoes before entering my home, and I ask that all visitors do the same. article: The people who design computers make them do lots of clever things to save power when they're running on battery power instead of AC. One of the things they do is run the processor more slowly, so that it uses less power. Just like driving your car at 130 miles per hour on the freeway will use more fuel than driving at 56 miles per hour on the freeway over the same distance, making the processor run slower will also use less power than running it faster. Similar tricks are done with other parts of the computer too, like turning off the hard disk if you don't use it for 30 seconds - spinning the disk inside a hard disk is a huge power drain.," "This is known as [frequency scaling] (URL0) or CPU throttling. The processor allows for separate'levels' of operation in which the frequency is adjusted. Your operating system determines that you are currently running on battery power, so it tries to reduce the energy consumed by lowering the frequency on the processor. When you plug the AC power back in, it bumps the frequency back up. This is done so that the consumer can continue using the laptop for longer. It would be quite annoying if your laptop ran out of power within half an hour. Your OS should also come with the option to avoid this sluggishness when on battery power. You will be able to go into something like'power options' and keep performance up even when on battery power, at the expense of having to recharge sooner. If you are on Windows 7, you can left click the battery icon in your system tray and choose'high performance' when you're on battery mode.

article: 5,000 years ago humans didn't know much about metal, metalworking, geology, or mining. But they did have a sense for fashion. Most metals exist naturally as rock. The metal atoms are connected to other kinds of elements like silicon and they don't look very interesting (to a non-geologist). In the world before the Bronze Age, the only metals most humans would recognize were silver and gold. Gold can be found as "nuggets" or "dust." The processes that bring it to the surface tends to deposit it in veins so that if you find some, you're likely to find more. Typically it is exposed by weather and flushed downhill into rivers, so finding gold means finding a river with some gold or silver in it, and then looking for more - you don't have to mine it. You can work gold without heat. It is "malleable" at room temperature, which means you can whack on it with hammers to change the shape of a lump of gold and bend it with tongs - and even though it is malleable it won't lose its new shape once you finish working it and that means you can make useful things. Gold will not hold an edge so it is useless as a blade. It is much denser than most other materials so it would make a good club, but you don't get much more head-bashing advantage with a gold cub than you would with stone or even wood. So other than as jewelry and as decoration, gold has little practical "use" to an ancient human. But it is pretty. Aesthetically gold looks "good" next to human skin tones. Why this is so is pretty much a mystery. But it's obvious that people found gold attractive very very early in human development. Who gets jewelry? Rich people. In the ancient world "rich" was defined as "don't have to farm." There were only three kinds of people like that: royalty, high priests, and successful generals. Since gold was in limited supply - but there was enough of it that people would recognize it and value it, and it wasn't good for any practical use, and as a metal it would "stay all in one place" and didn't have to be kept in jars or otherwise contained, it became a way for rich people to display their wealth. Gold is pretty easy to purify and to determine purity (it's a simple weightvolume calculation). That means that it could be exchanged between people for like value - a fixed amount of gold, of a certain purity, was "worth" some number of sheep or sheaves of wheat, or slaves, or land, or whatever. It became a unit of currency due to intrinsic properties convenient for anyone to access - all I need is a scale, a cup, some water, and a little math and I can figure out how much your gold is worth to me. 5,000 years of humans accepting gold as valuable has imbued it with a certain advantage vs. other similar metals. article: in photosystem II, a photon (packet of light energy) comes in and excites an electron (subatomic particle) in what's called a chlorophyll B molecule in the light harvesting complex. the excited electron is then passed through a series of electron carriers within the photosystem II complex, ultimately getting transferred to the reaction center chlorophyll molecule called P680. At this point, P680 has gained a high-energy electron that allows it to undergo oxidationreduction reactions, which results in the splitting of water molecules into oxygen, hydrogen ions, and electrons. The oxygen is released as a waste product, while the hydrogen and electrons are carried by specialized proteins to be used in the later stages of photosynthesis. Meanwhile, the high-energy electron from P680 is passed through a series of electron carriers within the photosystem II complex, ultimately getting transferred to photosystem I. This transfer of electrons generates ATP (adenosine triphosphate), a molecule that provides energy to the plant for various biological processes. Overall, photosystem II is an essential component of photosynthesis as it generates the energy-rich molecules needed for the later stages of the process.

article: It means a plasma that is made of quarks and gluons. It's a new form of matter because, under normal conditions, you cannot have a plasma made of quarks and gluons. I don't know why its direction of movement would be relevant.,Regular matter, the stuff we're made of, is mostly atoms. Atoms have protons, neutrons, and electrons. Usually, the electrons are zipping around the protons and there is an equal balance of electrons (negative charge) and protons (positive charge). Basically, every electron has a "home base" which is an atom or molecule. A "regular" plasma is when you heat up matter enough that the electrons go zipping out of their home bases and you have a soup of electrons and protons and stuff all mixed together. This requires very high temperatures, like in a blowtorch or on the surface of the Sun. Turns out that if you have enough energy in one place, the protons (and neutrons) themselves will split up into even smaller bits called quarks. Gluons are particles that hold quarks together (like glue. Yes, for real.). This requires INSANE amounts of energy, but it's what we think the universe was like right after the Big Bang. All of these random quarks can reconfigure into weird types of matter, so scientists can study what comes out to see what was happening during the plasma phase. TL:DR Heat stuff up enough and it "melts" into crazy tiny particles called quarks.

The breakdown voltage of water is very dependent on the purity of the water (and thus difficult to calculate) - the most pure water can have an extremely high resistance, somewhere on the order of 20 megohms, which gives a correspondingly high breakdown voltage. article: Humans are Trichomic, which is a fancy way to say that we see three primary colors. This is because we have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in the eye- one red, one green, and one blue. There is no way for us to see or perceive another primary color because it would require another type of cone cell to be present in our eyes. There are many animals that have a different number types of cone cells in their eyes. This allows them to see different primary colors than us. Dogs for example are Dichromic (2 colors), and birds are Tetrochromic (4 colors). Some species have even have more cone types than that. Fun fact: Goldfish are tetrochromic. They can see red, green, blue, and ultraviolet as their primary colors. Exactly how this is any use to them is unknown to me.','For some people there are 4 primary colors. See, the 3 primary colors, and the idea of color itself is a result of human biology. Most people have 3 different types of cone cells in their eyes. Each type of cell reacts to a different part of the light spectrum; red, green, and blue. Red, green and blue are the primary colors of additive colors, your monitor for instance has RGB LEDs. Subtraction colors like paints are the more familiar Red, Yellow, Blue. Some people, mostly women have 4 different cone cells in their eyes. This is called [tetrachromia] (URL0). Because of this they see a fourth primary color, probably yellow. This means that they can see more distinct shades of the colors we normally see. On a related note, women in general see more distinct shades of colors, particularly reds then men. The cornea; the translucent part of the eye blocks most ultraviolet light, and some people who have lost their corneas have reported seeing ultraviolet light. The mantis shrimp is an animal that can naturally see Ultraviolet light, giving it essentially a 4th primary color.','Well for the primary additive colors (red, green, and blue) they are our primary colors because we have three types of color sensors in our eyes - one that responds to red light, one to green, and one to blue. So were we to have a separate sensor specifically for Ultra-Violet, Yellow, or some other shade we would likely consider that to be a primary color.', "Yes! A fourth primary color can exist. The primary colors are due to the three colors that our our eyes can distinguish. Many animals can see in 4 colors, while some are colorblind. Some people even have genes for the green color receptor different enough that they see in 4 colors. The greens aren't quite separate, so it isn't like seeing a true 4th color, but it is different from typical 3 color sight.,The colors that can be described with Red Blue and Green are described with three axes L:the lightness, A: Yellow to Blue, B:Magenta to Cyan (a little bit simplified of an explanation). This is called the LAB color space and can describe any color using the primary colors Red Green and Blue (CyanGreenBlue, MagentaBlueRed). This system can be expanded to include any number of other colors it would just move the space to 4 dimensions instead of 3. article: Imagine that you worked in a filing facility - Your job is to take documents provided by various places and store them in your facility. Since you can't be there 247, you have a "work area" which consists of a desk where people can drop files off. When people have a document for you to file away, they leave it on this desk, and then when you see it you take it and place it back in storage. However, frequently people need to one: Get their document back, and two: Make changes and then send the file back to storage. This process is quite slow though: The person first has to leave a 'document request' form on the desk telling you what document they need. Then, when you come in and see it, you have to go back into storage, find the document, and leave it on the desk for them. Then they can take the document, make changes, and leave it back on the desk for you to find and store away again. The above isn't a huge problem if it's only a few documents, but you quickly find that lots of your customers are grabbing the same document over and over again, only to make a small change and put it back. This seems like a waste of time to you, because you end-up going to get the document from storage over and over again when-ever they need it. Thus, to remedy the problem, you add a 'fast-access' area to your desk, where you leave the most commonly or recently edited documents from each customer. That way, when a customer needs that document, they can just grab it right from there without having to go back into storage to get it. This all works fine to speed things up, and everybodies happy that the time to get a lot of their most recently used documents has gone from a day to instant access. But then a problem happens: The storage facility you're using decided to pack-up and move to a different location. It's not a huge problem, you just open a location for people to go and get their documents over there instead. However, some of your customers start complaining that you don't have all their documents. When you think about it, when the storage facility moved you never took all of the documents in the 'fast-access' area! Thus, you lost all those documents. To remedy the situation, you decide that the facility owner has to 'notify' you if they're going to move so you have time to move all of the documents in the 'fast-access' area into storage to prepare for the move. The above is basically how the OS handles your USB drive (the storage facility). USB drive access is fairly slow, with portable hard-drives even slower. To try and speed things up, the OS realizes that you have a few files that you either just edited, or are frequently editing, and keeps those files in memory (fast-access) instead of constantly writing it to your USB drive (which is slow). The problem is that if you remove your USB drive (move the storage facility), you lose the file's currently stored in memory unless you (the storage facility owner) notify the OS (the person handling the storage facility) that you're about to move the USB drive somewhere else.', "Computers use what's called a'write cache', which basically means that when something needs to be written, it isn't immediately written, but the computer waits a bit to see if more things need to be written, etc. Sort of like a bus waiting for more passengers before it departs. If you remove the USB too soon after you wrote something there, there is a chance that what you wanted to write is in the cache and hasn't been transferred yet.," "Disks are slow. To make your computer appear fast and responsive, operating systems don't write data to disk the instant you ask them to. They store the data in memory - this lets them quickly read the data if you ask for it again (a common operation), lets them only write to disk once if the same file is written to again (the new data overwrites data in memory) and lets the computer write the data to disk on a different thread instead of making your program wait. Ejecting a disk makes the operating system write all cached data to the disk. When it is done, then it puts up the message saying it is safe to remove.,More importantly, in this day and age, is safely ejecting a USB still matter? Even when enabled it's not really the issue. In general write caches aren't dumped hours or even minutes later, it's typically a matter of milliseconds to seconds. The actual reason is really simple. Each disk you have has a FAT - file allocation table. This is basically a telephone book of your hard disk. When you access a file your computer looks up its "number" (or numbers as your hard disk gets fragmented and it becomes impossible to store files in nice contiguous chunks) in the FAT and then reads it in. A similar process happens during writing except you actually have to write to the FAT as well. And this is the reason for safely ejecting. article: They float in water just like any other ship (or anything that floats in water) does: They sink to a level where the weight of the water they've displaced is equal to their own weight. After that, there's no overall force pulling them down any further. For something like a rock, if you weigh an amount of water taking up the same amount of space as that rock, you'll find that the water weighs less than the rock. So they'll just keep sinking. But for a block of (many kinds of) wood, the wood weighs less than the same volume of water. So the wood sinks into the water a little bit, but eventually reaches a point where it has displaced as much water as it itself weighs, and it stops sinking there. A big metal ship is kind of tricky, because your first thought is "but steel is heavier than water." And that's true. But they spread the weight of the steel out over so much volume that the overall density of the ship is less than water. So it acts just like the block of wood, not the rock. It's as if you hollowed out the block of rock - sure, the actual rock material itself is really dense, but the rock-plus-air-in-the-hollow-space is not.

When you develop a new technology, it's usually incredibly expensive to manufacturer the first batches of units because there are enormous capital costs associated with the research, development, and production of just the machines alone that will be used to actually manufacture those units. So initially, it may cost like 10x or even 100x the price of the conventional product to manufacture an equivalent product using the new technology. Obviously this is completely impractical and provides no real benefits. article: Running x86 on Arm is like trying to put diesel in a gas car - they're just not made to run it. Even if you're driving a car that's available in both forms, it won't work. The gear shift and brake pedals might be in the same spot but the engine won't run the same stuff. Different CPUs, different instructions, even if the OS provides the same system call interface. The way Android works around this is to run all your programs on a virtual machine. This is a program that'pretends' to be a CPU. You can compile a program to run on this virtual CPU and the program will run anywhere you've written your virtual machine.," "x86 and ARM are two different Instruction Set Architectures (ISAs). An ISA defines what operations a processor can perform. While x86 and ARM may share many instructions at an abstract level (add, subtract, branch, etc..), the actual opcodes (the 1s and 0s) used to make the processor execute work are not the same. When a program is compiled, it is translated into machine language, which consists of the instructions the processor can understand. If a program is compiled for the x86 ISA, an x86 processor will be able to execute the program. However, an ARM processor will have no idea what the program's instructions mean, because they aren't defined in the ARM ISA. The operating system handles many things programs need to execute, however instruction translation is not one of them.

article: So let's create an analogy where a computer is represented by a large hotel. The hotel has a street address, which is analogous to the computer's IP address. But if you want to communicate with a specific person at a hotel (send data to a specific program) you also need their room number (equivalent to the port number on a computer). So sending someone a message would be hotel street address room number (computer IP address port number). But most people use routers at home to let multiple computers access the Internet, and routers work by having their own IP address, and hiding all of the computers on your local network behind the router's IP address. So individual computers no longer have an externally-accessible IP address. In our analogy, this is like having a group of hotels all at the same street address. Internally, the people at the front desk refer to the various hotels as "Hotel A," "Hotel B," etc. But no one outside of the hotels know that, and even if they did, the standard way to write addresses on an envelope doesn't allow you to specify a sub-division like that; you can only have an address and a room number. So if I want to send a message to someone in room 1080 at a specific hotel, and both hotels have a room 1080, what do I do? Well, what if I set things up so that there are fake "room numbers" for the consolidated street address for my multiple hotels, and there's a rule book at the front desk that says "When someone sends a message to room 1080, forward it to room 1080 at hotel A. If someone sends a message to room 1088, forward it to room 1080 at hotel B. etc." That's port forwarding. The router maps its own ports to a port on a specific computer on your local network, and forwards any messages targeted at that port to the appropriate computer and port number on your internal network.

article: The math doesn't quite work that way. Some things scale up linearly, others to the second power (squared), others to the third power (cubed). If you merely double the size of everything (linearly), you won't end up with a correct, strong, and efficient design. In addition, some things will violate important physical constraints if doubled in size the oil may overheat and ignite, or the turbine blade tips may go supersonic causing destructive shock waves.," "No. If you make the plane twice as long, and scale up everything else on the plane to match, then the surface area of the plane will quadruple, but the volume (and weight) of the plane will octuple. This is because surface area depends on length (2), while volume depends on length (3). This scaling behavior is known as the [square-cube law] (URL0). Flying a plane depends on a careful balance between lift and weight. Lift depends on (among other things) surface area. So if you double the plane's size, your weight goes up faster than your lift does. This makes it no longer possible to fly, unless you change the actual design on the plane to increase lift somehow.,The short answer is "no, you can't simply scale up the size of a plane." The reason has to do with the interaction between surface area effects and volume effects. Surface area is a square function of length, while volume is a cube function of length; i.e. if you double the length, then the surface area is multiplied by four (22) while the volume is multiplied by eight (23). This means that when the length is doubled, the volume grows by twice as much as the surface area. Why is this relevant? Because the main thing that helps planes fly is lift provided by the wings, and lift is a function of surface area. The main thing that keeps planes from flying in the weight, and weight is a function of volume. So if you double the length scale of a plane, you're multiplying the surface area (and therefore lift) by four, but multiplying the volume (and therefore weight) by eight. The LiftWeight ratio is now 12 of what it was in the original plane, so it's probably not producing enough lift to fly. Of course, this is all an oversimplification. For one thing, it's not factoring in drag (which is a function of surface area) or the complex shape of a plane, but that's the simple gist of it.', "That's not how planes are made. The objective is to make them just strong enough to fly at minimum weight, as this maximizes operating efficiency. Even a 10 change in size would require some parts to be redesigned. article: A changing scope and 19th century tactics facing down 20th century realities. As originally conceived by Churchill (yes that Churchill) and his counterparts in the Navy, Gallipoli involved exactly zero ground troops. It was intended as a purely naval operation to force Turkey out of World War I and open up a new supply route to Russia. However, as the planning progressed, it became clear that the naval element would not be sufficient and that land forces would be necessary to achieve the objectives. This necessitated a major change in the scope of the operation and the deployment of troops. Unfortunately, the tactics employed by the Allied forces in Gallipoli were outdated and ill-suited to the realities of 20th-century warfare. The attack was launched with a massive frontal assault, relying on infantry charges and naval bombardment to soften up the Turkish defenses. This approach proved ineffective against the modern technologies and tactics employed by the Turkish defenders, who were able to inflict heavy casualties on the advancing Allied troops. Despite these challenges, the Allies persisted in their efforts, committing more troops and resources to the operation. However, the campaign ultimately failed to achieve its objectives, costing the lives of thousands of Allied troops and damaging the credibility of Churchill and his allies in the process. In hindsight, Gallipoli is widely regarded as a case study in the dangers of inflexible thinking and outdated tactics in the face of rapidly changing realities.
