article: Autonomous crop monitoring at high spatial and temporal resolution is a critical problem in precision agriculture. While Structure from Motion and Multi-View Stereo algorithms can finely reconstruct the 3D structure of a field with low-cost image sensors, these algorithms fail to capture the dynamic nature of continuously growing crops. In this paper we propose a 4D reconstruction approach to crop monitoring, which employs a spatio-temporal model of dynamic scenes that is useful for precision agriculture applications. Additionally, we provide a robust data association algorithm to address the problem of large appearance changes due to scenes being viewed from different angles at different points in time, which is critical to achieving 4D reconstruction. Finally, we collected a high quality dataset with ground truth statistics to evaluate the performance of our method. We demonstrate that our 4D reconstruction approach provides models that are qualitatively correct with respect to visual appearance and quantitatively accurate when measured against the ground truth geometric properties of the monitored crops.

article: In this paper, we study a posteriori error estimators which aid multilevel iterative solvers for linear systems of graph Laplacians. In earlier works such estimates were computed by solving a perturbed global optimization problem, which could be computationally expensive. We propose a novel strategy to compute these estimates by constructing a Helmholtz decomposition on the graph based on a spanning tree and the corresponding cycle space. To compute the error estimator, we solve efficiently a linear system on the spanning tree and then a least-squares problem on the cycle space. As we show, such estimator has a nearly-linear computational complexity for sparse graphs under certain assumptions. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

article: The snow wasn't cold, Anna thought, pressing her back hard against the concrete wall that protected her. It glided quiet to the ground around her, brushed her face, decorated her coat white as she waited. She tensed her thigh muscles again, trying to squeeze the ache from them. She didn't move. The side of the rifle was pressed against her stomach, still hot, the muzzle brushing the ground gathering the silent snow about it. It wasn't snow, she thought. The heat of the rifle would melt any snow near it. It was ash. Her team flowed through the environment around her, seen only in the brief expansion and contraction of dull shadows in the gloom. The bridge high above them brought an early dark to the area, revealing thin, dimming bars of dusk's light through to the ground around them. She could see her brother illuminated briefly in one of those beams as he slinked through one, his dogs loping behind him. Magnus was still there, at least, she told herself for the thousandth time. With all she had lost, with all they had all lost, they still had him. Bannon had thought them dead, either vaporized in the Chicago strike or the Purification that inevitably followed. The thousand false trails the Netcrawler had laid online had proven to work better than Anna had thought possible. Tracers pinged Magnus and his army in multiple areas around the Chicago area for over two months before the bomb. Men and women were even reported as seeing him in person walking the streets. It was enough for the President, apparently. The growing resistance had been ended almost as fast as it began, the Truth Dealers of the Official Media had broadcasted, casualties of the Nuke that somehow made it through the Patriot Field and destroyed the city. God's will, they called it. The OM had actually implied it was God himself who nuked the city to rid his burgeoning kingdom of its obdurate pestilence. Unauthorized media sources tore it to pieces, of course, and the Deep Web groaned and gnashed at the loss, and splinter cells were being formed all across the country in response. It all had worked almost too well. An army of 10,000 soldiers grew to 10 times that amount almost overnight. The army he had promised had been formed from his " death ," just as he said it would be. Magnus moved toward her position, the wet ground beneath him heard only when he drew very close. He was a soldier now. A leader. Her beautiful and goofy brother who could always make her laugh, who loved to dance as a child with his mother and father to mobile videos, who had a terrible voice but loved to sing, could now move through the dark like a cat. Could kill. The Army of the Penitent had set up under the causeway a few days after Purifying the areas headed toward New Orleans. They had clearly not expected resistance. Half their force was cut down before they could regather themselves and flee. Magnus would now order the rest slain. How cold he's become, she thought. She reached out to him as he neared, grabbing the back of his arm and pulling him close. He looked like he was made of bone in the dying light above. He spoke, his voice quiet but hard, " when you hear the dogs, begin. If they put up a fight for over two minutes, retreat and regroup and await my signal. Two minutes, no more. Set an alarm if you have to. We hit them good, I doubt they'll be much left to them after what we did earlier, but I'd like to prevent any more unnecessary casualties to our numbers if we can help it. " She gripped him harder, speaking a bit too loud, " What are we? " He just looked at her, blinking. " What are we, Magnus? Is this what we want to be? Are we any better than them if we Purge them like they do us? You wanted to be an actor, I wanted to help people. " " You are helping people, Anna. You're helping everyone that wanted to stand up against this but couldn't, or was too afraid to. " He stopped, stood upright. The dogs behind him sat in the wet earth, panting silently. " We're retribution, Anna. We're revenge, revenge for Mom, for Dad. Remembering what could have been will destroy you, as it almost destroyed me. I am not an actor, nor will I ever be. I am not a brother. Or a son. Not anymore. I am nothing more than the tip of a spear that was thrown the minute the Coup happened. It does no good to speak of roads not taken. "

article: We propose a novel mathematical framework to address the problem of automatically solving large jigsaw puzzles. This problem assumes a large image which is cut into equal square pieces that have been randomly shuffled. The objective is to recover the original image by arranging the pieces in a correct order. Our proposed framework consists of the following steps: 1. Feature Extraction: We extract certain features from each square piece of the jigsaw puzzle using computer vision techniques. These features can be color histograms, edge information, texture information, or any other suitable feature. 2. Similarity Matrix Construction: We construct a similarity matrix that quantifies the similarity between every pair of square pieces in the jigsaw puzzle. The similarity between two pieces is determined by comparing the features extracted in step 1. 3. Clustering: We apply clustering algorithms to group the most similar pieces together. We can use any clustering algorithm such as k-means, hierarchical clustering, or spectral clustering. 4. Graph Construction: We create a graph where each node represents a cluster of similar square pieces. The edges between the nodes represent the similarity between clusters. 5. Graph Matching: Finally, we use graph matching algorithms to match the nodes of the graph to the correct order and orientation of the original image. Our proposed framework has shown promising results on solving large jigsaw puzzles automatically. However, there are still challenges to be addressed, such as handling different types of jigsaw puzzles, dealing with missing pieces or noisy data, and improving the efficiency of the algorithm for real-world applications.

article: I felt as if I was somehow being punished. For my hero apprenticeship I was assigned to one of the least exciting and meticulous heroes from the previous generation: the Trapper. "Ugh, how long is this old buffoon going to take on setting this trap, eh? We've been here configuring this pulley-leveraged netting apparatus going on 2 hours now," I would think to myself, as I passed him the various tools he needed. He usually sang a gentle tune to himself in-between orders given to me, while I would sit in an agitated state, contemplating on how I should be flying through town engaging in significant and exciting hand-to-hand combat sequences. I envisioned all the fantastical ways we could be catching criminals instead of these mundane elaborate traps. And even after we had a criminal under arrest, the Trapper felt the need to lecture the bloke on his wrongs. Alarmingly, he was almost gentle with them, a support for them. I was the best fighter in my graduating class. I have lighting quick reflexes, super strength, and the ability to fly over short distances. Think of me as a poor man's Superman. Still, to be even mentioned within the same sentence as the all time great is no insignificant feat. All my classmates knew I was bound for grand things, so too did my hero teachers. Or at least I thought they did, for why would they punish me, sentence me to spend long, boring days with the old Trapper? There were a few moments throughout the week that I would look forward to - those rare opportunities that I got to take the initiative. The old Trapper would allot 2-3 criminal apprehensions per week, which he would preside over. He never joined in on the old-fashioned ass kicking. It was fine to me; more for me. He never came right out and said it, but I always felt as if he was slightly disappointed by the way I handled these situations. " You are much stronger than these gentlemen here. But do you always need to show it fully? ," he asked once. I never understood him. These were bad men that committed heinous crimes. They deserve nothing but pain. We set off one day to one what I figured to be a normal day. He took me aside at the start, however, and said, " I want to show you something today, something different. There will be no arrests made today. " Great... here we go. Just when I thought this couldn't get any less exciting, the old geezer is going to show me some Middle Eastern meditation techniques or how to cross-stitch or something unfathomably boring. I was surprised when he pulled up to the joint correction facility and prison. " I thought we weren't working today? Not arresting any criminals? " " We aren't arresting any. We are going to pay visits to some. " Oh boy. We went through the back of the complex with no troubles from the guards, who gave us praise as we strolled through the corridors. The Trapper led me to one cell, one obviously predetermined by the directness we approached it. I looked into and saw it was a criminal I had previously apprehended. He was hunkered down in a corner muttering some imperceptible words. I swelled up with pride, hid it on the outside. " So this is one less piece of garbage on the streets. Job well done, right? ," I asked. " A piece of garbage, yes, with no hope to be recycled, " the Trapper said cryptically. I was confused. " Have a conversation with this man " said the Trapper. What was this guy getting at here? I approached the jail cell more nervously than a hero should ever be, especially considering my foe was behind bars. " Ahem, hey you. Yes, you. I would like to speak with you. " The figure's head swiveled fast and glared right at me. He stood up strode over to me and began cursing obscenities, with spittle flying from his mouth in his fit of rage. I tried to quiet him, to get him to speak normally, but no amount of imploring worked. The Trapper grabbed me by the arm, led me away from the cell to another one in the correctional portion of the facility. This time, he walked right up to the cell and began conversing with its inhabitant. It was a criminal he had brought down a few weeks back. His continence, his whole body seemed to exuberate happiness. He filled the Trapper in on how well his recovery had been going and thanked him for visiting him again. Afterwards, the Trapper looked me dead in the eye and said, " While he may be an anomaly, he would never be what he is today - a better man fighting for a second chance - without consideration from someone, anyone. These men have nothing. Beating and reducing them to rubble does nothing for them. It would be better to just off them. They became more wretched and perpetually involved in the system. There is no escape from their hell. But sometimes, even if it is 1 out of a 1,000, there is a break through and they can make change. One life saved is worth a world entire. " I still use my powers in the only way I know how, with physicality, but I only use the necessary force to take a perp down. No more, no less. And I attempt to guide them afterwards, not throw them into a landfill. Man can be recyclable, no matter how rare it is.

article: Capturing the essence of a textile image in a robust way is important to retrieve it in a large repository, especially if it has been acquired in the wild (by taking a photo of the textile of interest). In this paper we show that a texel-based representation fits well with this task. In particular, we refer to Texel-Att, a recent texel-based descriptor which has shown to capture fine grained variations of a texture, for retrieval purposes. article: Many computer vision and medical imaging problems are faced with learning from large-scale datasets, with millions of observations and features. In this paper we propose a novel efficient learning scheme that can handle such large datasets. Our approach is based on the use of deep learning techniques, specifically a deep neural network architecture called a convolutional neural network (CNN), and a training strategy called stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with mini-batch updates. The CNN framework is particularly suited to handling high-dimensional data, such as images, and has demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in many computer vision tasks. The key idea behind CNNs is to leverage the local and spatial correlation of image pixels by using convolutional filters that extract meaningful features across the image. SGD is an optimization algorithm commonly used for training deep neural networks. It works by iteratively adjusting the weights of the network in the direction of the negative gradient of a loss function, with the aim of minimizing the loss. As the name suggests, SGD updates the weights in a stochastic manner by sampling a subset of the data (called a mini-batch) for each iteration, which reduces the computational cost and enables efficient processing of large-scale datasets. Our proposed learning scheme combines the power of CNNs and SGD with mini-batch updates to efficiently learn from large-scale datasets in a scalable and effective manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by evaluating it on two challenging datasets: the ImageNet dataset for object recognition, and the LIDC-IDRI dataset for lung nodule detection in CT images. Our results show that our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Overall, our proposed efficient learning scheme can be a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners working on large-scale computer vision and medical imaging problems.

The tiny amount one picks up by touching a pile of cocaine with one's fingertip isn't enough to do anything serious, but it's enough to cause brief, local numbness on the tongue. It's one of the only white, powdery substances that can do that, so it's a quick and accurate way of determining whether the perp has a bag of coke or something innocuous (e.g., powdered sugar, baking powder, etc.). Believe it or not, unlike most street drugs, cocaine isn't a schedule I substance (i.e., totally illegal with no recognized clinical use). It's schedule II (i.e., rigorously controlled, but available via prescription). It's still occasionally used as a topical anesthetic in sinus surgeries. It is no longer the preferred agent most of the time, but there are apparently certain situations where it's the right tool for the job, as it were. Many ENT (i.e., Ear, Nose and Throat) surgical clinics will have a supply of it on-hand at all times. But second, law enforcement doesn't use this method of field testing nearly as often as it used to. And it probably never used it as much as movies and TV shows would lead one to believe. Why? Because having a cop take a quick taste of a suspicious powder is visually effective and quick. Waiting for them to bust out a field chemical testing kit (or, even worse waiting for one to arrive on the scene from somewhere else), and then watching someone perform the relevant chemical test, is boring, both visually and dramatically. Chemical testing kits are cheaper and more widely available than they were fifty years ago, so there's even less reason for actual cops to do this today than there ever was.

article: In this work, we introduce an algorithmic approach to generate microvascular networks starting from larger vessels that can be reconstructed without noticeable segmentation errors. Contrary to larger vessels, the reconstruction of fine-scale components of microvascular networks shows significant segmentation errors, and an accurate mapping is time and cost intense. Thus there is a need for fast and reliable reconstruction algorithms yielding surrogate networks having similar stochastic properties as the original ones. The microvascular networks are constructed in a marching way by adding vessels to the outlets of the vascular tree from the previous step. To optimise the structure of the vascular trees, we use Murray's law to determine the radii of the vessels and bifurcation angles. In each step, we compute the local gradient of the partial pressure of oxygen and adapt the orientation of the new vessels to this gradient. At the same time, we use the partial pressure of oxygen to check whether the considered tissue block is supplied sufficiently with oxygen. Computing the partial pressure of oxygen, we use a 3D-1D coupled model for blood flow and oxygen transport. To decrease the complexity of a fully coupled 3D model, we reduce the blood vessel network to a 1D graph structure and use a bi-directional coupling with the tissue which is described by a 3D homogeneous porous medium. The resulting surrogate networks are analysed with respect to morphological and physiological aspects.

article: They took my mother from our house, though I cried and begged them not to. The doctors were confused. This was an illness they had never seen before. My mother did not move or speak or even draw a breath, no matter what they did to her. Her skin was pale and cold; her eyes, when they drew the eyelids up, were still and did not respond to light or movement. She had begun to smell, too, a harsh reeking scent that lingered in her sickbed long after she had been taken from it. At the hospital, they treated her poorly. The room they gave her was small and poorly lit, tucked away in a corner of the building. The nurses brought her neither food and water to make her stay more comfortable nor medicine to hasten her recovery. Each day I sat by her side and waited for the healing that was inevitable and yet seemed so far off. Their treatment of my mother made me angrier and angrier and angrier, until at last, one bright morning, I pulled her limp form the bed, sure that I could care for her just as well at home as these fools could here. I wish I had not. When I touched her, her flesh was loose and ripe and sagging. The stench was overwhelming, and only grew stronger as I tried to wrap my arms around her. And- and when- It pains me to form the words. I can not talk about what I saw that day without seeing it once again in my mind. But you deserve to know. When I pulled my mother from the bed, the skin of her face, her eyes, her lips- it split. And within her were worms, white and squirming, making a meal of her flesh. I remember little beyond that; it is all bits of memory and flashes of emotion, blurred together in my mind. I know I screamed and brought the doctors running, and then fought them until they were forced to sedate me. I know that when I was brought to, my mother..... no. Not my mother. What was left of my mother, the thing that sat in the hospital bed- it was gone. They had taken it, to where I do not know. They told me not to speak of what had happened to anyone, on pain of a thousand years' imprisonment. But I must tell you, so that when the time comes you will not be so terrified as I was. I can feel it. There is a heaviness pressing down on me, a stiff sour coldness in my limbs that I have never felt before. When I saw what had happened to my mother- what had become of her- something changed within me. The worm are inside me, too. I can feel them when I sleep, their tiny bodies burrowing phantom holes all through me. I know not how long it will take- days or months or decades- but somebody I will become like my mother, gone somewhere far away with nothing but meat and worms left where I once was. When that time comes, do not wait by my bedside. I do not want you to see what will become of me. I do not want the worms to burrow their way into you.

article: We study the following variant of the classic bin packing problem. The input is a set of items I {1, ..., N } with corresponding sizes s 1, ..., s N, where each item size is a positive integer between 1 and B. The goal is to pack the items into the minimum number of bins of capacity C, such that the total size of items assigned to each bin does not exceed the bin capacity. There are different algorithms to solve this problem, but one common approach is called the First Fit Decreasing (FFD) algorithm. Here's how it works: 1. Sort the items in decreasing order based on their size. 2. Take the first item and try to place it in the first bin. 3. If the item fits, add it to the bin and move to the next item. 4. If the item does not fit, try the next bin. 5. If no bin can accommodate the item, open a new bin and add the item to it. 6. Repeat steps 3-5 for the remaining items. This algorithm has a worst-case complexity of O (N log N), where N is the number of items. However, in practice, it can be more efficient than other algorithms due to its simplicity and good performance on realistic inputs.

article: Android applications (and apps in other operating systems) operate on a message queue. The operating system sends messages to the app, such "the user tapped the screen at x,y" or "the use clicked the back button." The app has a single main thread that handles these messages. Whenever it reads a message, it executes the code that handles this message (if there is any) and when finished it will notify that operating system that the message has been handled, and asks for the next one. "Application not responding" happens when the application takes too long to handle a message. The OS will see that it didn't receive a notification that the message has been handled, and will realize there's something wrong. Exiting the app happens from within - the app finishes up its tasks (saving data, closing connections, cleaning up files) and tells the OS "I'm done." The OS then removes the app from memory. Killing the app is forcing the app to shutdown from the outside - the OS simply destroys the app, automatically freeing any resources that it was keeping.

article: The multi-valued logic of ukasiewicz is a substructural logic that has been widely studied and has many interesting properties. It is classical, in the sense that it admits the axiom schema of double negation elimination, [ DNE ] . However, our understanding of ukasiewicz logic can be improved by separating its classical and intuitionistic aspects. The intuitionistic aspect of ukasiewicz logic is captured in an axiom schema, [ CWC ] , which asserts the commutativity of a weak form of conjunction. We explain how this axiom is equivalent to a restricted form of contraction. We then show how ukasiewicz Logic can be viewed both as an extension of classical affine logic with [ CWC ] , or as an extension of what we call intuitionistic ukasiewicz logic with [ DNE ] , intuitionistic ukasiewicz logic being the extension of intuitionistic affine logic by the schema [ CWC ] . At first glance, intuitionistic ukasiewicz logic seems to be a very weak fragment of intuitionistic logic. We show that [ CWC ] is a surprisingly powerful (restricted) form of contraction, implying for instance all the intuitionistically valid De Morgan's laws. However the proofs can be very intricate. These results are presented using derived connectives to clarify and motivate the proofs. Applications include: a simpler proof of the Ferreirim-Veroff-Spinks theorem, proof that idempotent elements of a hoop form a sub-hoop, proof that double negation is a hoop homomorphism, and proofs for the above mentioned De Morgan dualities. We conclude by showing that our homomorphism result on the double-negation mapping in particular implies that all negative translations of classical into intuitionistic ukasiewicz coincide (as they do in full intuitionistic logic). This is in contrast with affine logic for which we show, by appeal to results on semantics proved in a companion paper, that both the Gentzen and the Glivenko translations fail.

article: ' Forget about it,'said Neil. ' This is hopeless.' The room fell silent for a couple more minutes. It didn't feel like talking back to Neil. He was too peculiar of a character. ' You know, I have no clue. I just have no clue. I swear to God...' Somewhere high above, God pretended to be absolutely deaf as Neil cursed the foundations of the earth on which he was now standing with phrases more fitting for a whaling ship captain than a second-year mathematics student. Everything went silent again. Neil stood up and walked around the table. A window in a desperate need of cleaning was barely letting through enough sunlight to illuminate the papers. Dust floated in the air much the same way smoke hangs around in bad fanfiction. Neil was miserable. In his life, there had been many problems, big, small, and somewhere in-between. Neil liked to classify them by rank and size. Set theory, however, did not fall on the spectrum, being an ever-present nightmare that was so far off the scale it was hard to place it with any certainty. What made it worse was that set theory had its own logic and its own rules. The logic was madness and the rules were fake, Neil was certain, but he could sense there was something. There was definitely something. Perhaps it was the metallic taste of death he felt every time he looked at the phrase " complex numbers ." He just couldn't place his finger on it. And today he was so close he could almost feel the thread of mathematical thought slip through his hands and trail away, mocking him. He was always one step behind. Set theory was winning. ' Screw it,'he whispered. It was time to get going anyway. The exam was not going to write itself. He made one last desperate circle around the room and opened the door to the kitchen. In front of him was a small hill of a desk. Neil blinked. A small ball of dust floated above his head. Neil blinked again. The ball was still there. He stepped forward. Above him, a huge cathedral-sized window was letting through huge cathedral-sized shards of light. Neil swore to himself quietly, suddenly afraid to disturb the silence. ' Hello? Anybody there?' The room didn't answer. At this point, it was quite certain that there was something wrong with Neil. For starters, he was too small. Neil ran to the desk, and then made his way across the room to the bigger version of the door he just walked through seconds ago. It felt solid. Menacingly solid. He pushed it. With a creak mixed in with Neil's curses to the heavens, the door swung on its hinges, opening up into a valley of a study room. The dark brown mountain towered high above Neil. A cloud of dust had the look of a hundred small sheep prepared to rain oblivion on a traveler. Light was falling with the heaviness of a truck of bricks. Neil looked around in disbelief and sat down. He was definitely going to be late for his test. Far above, God smiled. He alone knew the rules, and he didn't care enough to explain them to a human, even if a human was capable of making perfect fractals.

article: Puerto Rico has been an unincorporated territory of the USA since 1898 when it was taken from the Spanish after the Spanish-American war. article: Sure. You've very likely eaten cancerous cells in your life. But there's a few things that prevent it from forming cancers in our own bodies. First, we don't use their DNA. We use our own. Theirs is incompatible and so our cells don't use it for instructions. Next, it doesn't get into our cells intact in the first place. Our body digests cells and breaks them down, killing them and destroying their genetic instruction sets. Then the proteins, minerals, carbohydrates, fats and other stuff in them get delivered via bloodstream to where it's needed. The faulty DNA in those cells doesn't survive the conversion and trip. In a sense, it's like dismantling a lego model so you can put it back in its original box, then using the pieces to build something else instead later.," "Well the good news is that you won't get cancer by eating cancer cells. Now, an interesting aside that is related to this question I think - there is a way you can contract a disease by eating other tissue that isn't filled with bacteriavirus - called prion disease. Prion diseases are usually spontaneous, with one protein in the brain malfolding to cause problems. Creutzfelt-Jacob Disease (CJD) is the classic example of this, and it is very rare. [Kuru] (URL1) and [Mad Cow Disease] (URL0) can be contracted when you consume animal or human parts that are contaminated by these malformed proteins. Speculation is that CJD victims in Papua New Guinea were consumed by family members in tribal cannibalism funeral tradition and this led to an epidemic of prion disease. So your line of thinking is what led people to determine that this disease could be transmissible - something people took decades to figure out.," "Yes, and nothing. Cancerous tissue is just tissue that grows uncontrollably, it's still edible. It might not taste like the thing you're eating though (most likely an organ like the liver) because cancerous cells often undergo chemical changes compared to the tissue they emerged from. Once we ingest the tumor, it will get digested, broken down and destroyed. Even if somehow there were living cells in the tumor and somehow some of them found their way into our bloodstream they would swiftly be destroyed. Cancer is dangerous because it arises from the host's own tissues, which prevents the host's immune system from recognizing it as a threat. Foreign tissues, especially foreign animal tissues, would be recognized as a threat and destroyed.,Eating cancerous cells is like shredding a car with ignition problems. The car shredder will not inherit the ignition issues of the cars it shreds. In just the same way as you will not get cancer from eating cancerous cells. Your digestion system is taking the food apart molecule by molecule and filtering out the small components to be later reassembled into other products. The DNA of a cancer cell will be broken into its component nuclear acid groups which destroys the cancer and any other signs of life.', "Nothing. It gets digested. Digested tissue isn't going to still be alive and reproducing. While there are some cancers that are transmissible in animals, it is rare, and very very rare in humans, and involves transmission of the malignant cells, not broken down dead ones.,I have heard about these HeLa cancer cells, which supposedly can keep dividing forever. article: I'm assuming you're asking something like: Why does a 3TB drive cost more than a 2TB drive and the answer is yes, there are material costs involved. First take into consideration what a hard drive is made of: Enclosure (the casing) Controller (that green thingy on the bottom) Drive Platters (basically shiny discs that actually store your data) Drive Head Etc (How the drive is read) The enclosure and drive head are pretty unimportant in this argument since they rarely change between drive types. What increases the cost is usually in the controller and the drive platters. Let's start with platters. Each platter has a certain physical capacity. Say for example you can fit 1GB of data onto a platter It would take 1000 of these to be able to store 1TB there's no physical way you could fit 1000 of these into a hard drive (which has certain height, length, width restrictions). So, you'll need to engineer some way to fit more space on a platter. You spend on research and development and finally (years later) you figure out how to get a whopping 250GB per platter. Now you can take 4 of these put them together to get 1TB. But.... you just spent a fortune figuring out how to store more data on these platters. So how do you recoup your costs? Make the price higher the high price reflects the huge investment made in figuring out how to make the drive in the first place. This is also why the price decreases as times goes by. The technology is mostly established for that drive, there's no more costs involved other than production (and occasional maintenance). Now, on to the controller. The controller, as the name might imply, controls how the data is read or written to the drive; it's the interface for your computer to talk to a hard drive. Imagine you spend very little on making a controller. All it does is blindly read and write data there's no error checking. So if by some weird mishap data becomes corrupt, it won't bother telling you or even noticing. Sounds like a pretty shitty drive, right? Well, that's why a lot of work goes into making more robust controllers that are catered to the drive. A specific hard drive model will probably have a completely custom controller that cannot be swapped with the controller for a different hard drive model. And this, again, goes back to the R D in making said controller. After those factors, there's also supply and demand to take into consideration. Spinny drives on the smaller side have a smaller amount of demand, so supply is usually limited which drives the price up a bit. So the price per GB is usually higher than larger sized drives.," "Yes there are also actual material costs, but mostly it's because the data on a hard drive has to be organized by controller electronics, and the more data is there to manage, the more complex that controller has to be. EDIT: because the reply to this was buried, but it did make me bring up this point: Apart from the electronics, if you want to double the capacity of a hard drive, you need either double the medium to store the data on or store the data at double density, requiring more expensive readwrite hardware.,Additionally there are R D costs and investment that went to the production of that hard drive. Actually same is true for all high tech stuff.', "One simple reason is hard drives often have a different number of [platers and heads] (URL0) inside (you can see them better in [this image] (URL1) stacked one on top of the other) If a single platter can hold 1TB, then you may find a 1TB drive has just 1 platter, a 2TB drive has 2 platters and a 3TB drive has 3 platters etc. Alternatively a 1TB drive may have 2 500GB platters because 500GB platters don't have to be as precise and can be made cheaply, or they have a lot of old 500GB platters they want to use up.," "Let's say we compare a 128gb and 256gb solid state drive. Besides R D is there that much of a difference in manufacturing cost?,It's a combination of technology and market. Higher density devices cost more to manufacture. That's true for every device. Smaller parts, tighter tolerances, higher quality control, etc. But market costs come into play, too. The top of the line leading edge technology will be sold in smaller numbers and the price will be high. Limited competition, sales, etc. That would be the high-capacity drives. Once they've been out for awhile, the prices drop. Stores now have them in stock and want to move them out. Price is constantly dropping, so stores want to move their inventory before they lose profits. What's interesting is that the curve of cost (per MB) vs capacity has an "elbow" to it. The highest capacity (highest density) drives make up a sharp increase in price per MB. The LOWEST capacity drives, strangely, ALSO make up an increased price per MB. That's because those drives reached a minimum price and stores stopped discounting them. They may have even stopped stocking them. When buying a drive, you likely want to pick the saddle of that cost-per-MB curve. You want a drive that has a high enough density that the cost per MB is low, but not so high that you pay the premium for top-of-the-line new technology.', "For drives that are relatively close in size it doesn't have anything to do with material cost as they are all the same. Manufacturing things like hard drives in a consistent manner is rather difficult. To deal with this the factories build all one size drive, lets say 5TB. After they are built they run them through a set of tests. Some drives will reliably spin faster than others so they get a 7200 RPM rating. The slower ones get a 5400 RPM rating. Some will have 4TB of usable space and some will only have 1TB. What the drive ends up being sold as just depends on how it tests and what firmware is written to it. Drives that may meet requirements but not very well are sent to Walmart. The same thing happens with computer processors. They sell 3 core processors but that is just so they can do something with the 4 core ones they make that have a core that doesn't work so well.," "Why something costs X can be summed up in three words: Demand and Supply Since the supply side has been covered below, I'll talk about demand. Demand in economics shows how much people in economics are willing to pay for something. How much they are willing to pay for something depends upon the size of the benefit they can get from that something. Since people can get more benefit from a 1TB hard-drive, than say a 500GB one, they are willing to pay more for them, and therefore, the 1TB hard drive will cost more.,I bring up the same scenario with motorcycles. A 250cc motorcycle can cost thousands more than a 125cc motorcycle, even though only a few minor things in the engine are different. The manufacturing process of these bikes are identical. You may even say that the 250cc should be less expensive since they outsell them 2:1.

article: "Nah," I said, tossing back the last of my bourbon. "In fact I don't even remember what I did." The bar was dimly lit, too loud, too hot. Stereotypical sort of place for a stereotypical sort of guy and I motioned to the bartender for another and he took his goddamn time before coming down to my side of the bar. The girl beside me, she was asking me all sorts of stupid questions. Asking about who I was, where I'd been. She'd been asking about my divorce, about why it ended, about what she'd done and what I'd done and wanting me to wrap up years worth of experience into a single tidy succinct statement about what my contribution to the downfall had been. Did I still think about it? Ha. Did I still think about it. Every goddamn day and the bartender refilled my drink and I downed it and I mumbled, another, and the girl beside me laughed and said, "Damn, you really like that whiskey." What had I done? Shit. Love isn't an hour-and-a-half chick flick with a clear theme. Love isn't a science that can be easily modeled. Love is a messy web of comments and gestures, of sweet kisses and bitter arguments, of differences and solutions and broken doors and hearts and fist-shaped holes through walls. Love wasn't a battleground it was the battle. It was as fluid and unpredictable as a waterfall and I hadn't figured out any other end to it but the rocks below where the water inevitably crashes and the river picks up the pieces. So what had I done? I motioned to the bartender, who was trying his best to ignore me as he hit on a couple of young, hot blondes who laughed at his jokes down on the other side of the bar and I murmured hardly loud enough for anybody to hear, "another." So what had I done? I don't know. Years of trying to improve myself. Years of tearing myself down with alcohol. Years of fighting the good fight, whatever the fuck that was. Years of trying to make it work. Years of thinking of myself. The bartender refilled my drink once again, god bless his pretty little soul, and the girl beside my yammered on about something and I nodded in quiet contemplation but the only thought in my mind was her original question of, "Do you still think about what you did?" What did she know about what I'd done. What could she possibly know? Was I selfish? Sure. But who wasn't? Love is a tug-of-war of wills, a battle between the strong and the weak, and when that equilibrium is suddenly upturned and the rope starts making headway in your opponent's direction, that's when things get real messy. And they had. And I'd reacted like any self-respecting man would. With broken vases and insults hurled like bullets from a sling and quick jabs to innocent walls who'd never even seen it coming. So what had I done? I'd destroyed that house, that quaint little piece-of-shit house that we'd spent years building. I'd torn it down and seen how cheaply-made it all was, how little value there was in the scraps. I'd thrown the photo albums in the trash because memories are as good as the moldy leftovers in the fridge when it all comes crashing down anyway. What had I done? What had she done? The answers to these questions would take five years to tell. It was not as neatly-packaged of an answer as the girl at the bar beside me would like to hear. "You wan na get out of here?" she asked. "Yeah," I said, resigning myself to whatever the next rollercoaster of lust and love and self-destruction had to offer me. "Yeah, I do."

article: Reinforcement learning requires manual specification of a reward function to learn a task. Furthermore, the exploration-exploitation trade-off, where the agent must balance exploring new actions and exploiting known ones, can be difficult to manage in practice. article: Seven men, all wearing matching black gear and equipped with high powered weaponry, stood at attention inside a large dark hangar in front of a large black helicopter. Two additional men entered from a nearby door and walked towards the lineup. One of the two wore matching gear to the original seven including the assault rifle and ammo harness, but the other man was only wearing the black skin tight shirt, black cargo pants, black combat boots but was carrying a file folder. The man with combat gear joined the seven at attention while the other addressed them. "Gentlemen. This is Jack Johnson. He'll be replacing Mark Peters, may god rest his soul. Unfortunately we don't have time for drills to integrate Jack into the team correctly. Luckily however, Jack is specialized in long range and solo operations which he'll be performing in this mission, so the camaraderie can wait. As you're aware we have a mission, but what you're not aware of, is that it's not a standard operation. Your current gear will have to be returned to the quartermaster. Your equipment should be arriving shortly. I want you out front in fifteen." the commander ordered. The men scattered and began removing their gear and placing it on a table near a large caged off room in the corner of the hanger. "So, Jack..... Solo and long range ops. That's like a sniper right?" The shortest of the eight asked. "Yeah. Forty-eight solo missions, ninety-two confirmed kills." Jack replied. "Impressive, Mark only had nineteen confirmed kills when he started. I'm Frank, this is Jeff, Mark Rodrigez AKA M.K. 2, Rod McGavin, Kyle, Kilroy and tiny over there is Oscar." the short man finished. "I'm looking forward to working with you." Jack continued. "Introduced and immediately sent into a mission, that's not common is it?" "No." Answered Jeff "I've been doing this for almost fourteen years and it's never happened before. Usually they'd send the Bravo, Charlie, Delta or Echo. Something big must be happening." "Hey newbie, what do you prefer, Laser, Plasma or good ol' fashioned lead?" Mark asked. "Being a long range specialist, Laser. But each one has their advantages and disadvantages and I'm perfectly capable of using whatever is required for the situation." Jack stated flatly as if it were a programmed response. "Already you sound just like Peters. Me, I'm a plasma man. Just got ta tag them and they burn up into dust." Mark continued. "Shame plasma and laser weaponry is too expensive for standard issue." Rod joked. "This job would be easy as hell if we didn't have to aim for a target the size of a coconut every time we fired." The group shared a laugh and headed towards the exit. Outside the eight men stood at attention as a military convoy of four military escort vehicles surrounding a large supply rig pulled up to the hangar. The commander walked towards the convoy and displayed his military credentials, signed some papers on the clipboard and ordered the crew to unload the rig. "Alright soldiers, Mission briefing. As you know this isn't some minor event. We're effectively a man down due to lack of squad training, but this is an emergency situation. We'll be rendezvousing with Bravo, Charlie, Delta and Echo. Military intelligence found a dragon." the commander stated. "Get your gear and get on the chopper, we head out in one hour." The men walked over to the equipment boxes unloaded off the supply truck. Each one labelled with a name. Jack found the one labeled Mark Peters and opened it. Inside was a weapon that was like nothing he's ever seen. "What the hell is this? This isn't a plasma weapon, it doesn't have any heating coils. It also has an ammo system, so it's not a laser weapon. No hammer or anything so it's definitely not lead." he asked quietly to no one in particular. "That is the Magnetized Near Light Speed Projectile System. AKA a railgun. You ever use one before?" The commander interrupted. "No sir." Jack replied standing at attention. "You know how to use a laser rifle right? It's the same principle, just that there's a massive kick after. I hope you didn't have plans on using your shoulder for the next week." The commander quipped sarcastically. "No sir." Jack remained at attention. "There's instructions in the box, read them and familiarize yourself with the weapon. You'll need it." The commander said solemnly. "Yes sir." Jack stated. The commander walked off towards Kilroy, past Oscar and Frank. "Hey, Oscar. What's..... what's going on? I've killed some weird stuff, but what's this about a Dragon?" Jack called over to Oscar. "You know how sometimes Undead can get stuck together or just attach an extra limb to themselves? So you get like, something with four arms?" Oscar asked. "Yeah." Jack replied. "Well, an egg is when you get like hundreds of bodies all fusing together without thought. Eggs aren't a problem because they fuse in a way that makes it unable to move, it's just a big ball of flesh, you start it on fire or whatever and it's done. A dragon is like that but instead of fusing randomly, it fuses intelligently leaving you with a giant undead monster that's capable of doing serious damage and withstanding most weaponry. The danger is that it's smart enough to ditch limbs that are on fire, so even using plasma weapons isn't super effective against it. If it's large enough it'll take way too long to kill. article: The Dubins Traveling Salesman Problem (DTSP) has generated significant interest over the last decade due to its occurrence in several civil and military surveillance applications. Currently, there is no algorithm that can efficiently solve DTSP for all cases. However, there are several approaches that can provide relatively good solutions. One approach is to use heuristics, which are fast and practical methods that do not guarantee optimal solutions but can provide good solutions in reasonable time. Examples of heuristics for DTSP include the Nearest Neighbor algorithm, the Approximate Minimum Spanning Tree algorithm, and the 2-Opt algorithm. Another approach is to use metaheuristics, which are optimization algorithms that can search through large solution spaces and find good solutions. Examples of metaheuristics for DTSP include the Genetic algorithm, the Simulated Annealing algorithm, and the Ant Colony Optimization algorithm. Finally, there are also exact algorithms that can solve DTSP optimally for small instances. One example is the cutting-plane algorithm, which is based on linear programming. Another example is the branch-and-bound algorithm, which is a tree-based search algorithm that allows for pruning infeasible solutions. The choice of algorithm depends on the size of the problem, the required solution quality, the available computational resources, and the specific constraints of the application.

article: The motivation for this paper is to apply Bayesian structure learning using Model Averaging in large-scale networks. Currently, Bayesian model averaging algorithm is applicable to networks with only tens of nodes, and its scalability to larger networks is limited. However, with the explosion of data in various fields, such as social networks, genetics, and neuro-imaging, there is a need for scalable Bayesian structure learning methodologies for large-scale networks. The objective of this paper is to propose a scalable Bayesian model averaging algorithm for large-scale networks, which can handle hundreds or thousands of nodes. The proposed algorithm is based on a divide-and-conquer approach, where the network is partitioned into smaller sub-networks, and the Bayesian model averaging algorithm is applied to each sub-network. Then, the sub-networks are merged to obtain the final Bayesian model. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on synthetic and real-world networks, and compared with existing Bayesian model averaging algorithms. The results show that the proposed algorithm provides accurate and efficient results for large-scale networks, while existing algorithms fail to scale up. Overall, this paper contributes to the development of scalable Bayesian structure learning methodologies for large-scale networks, which can benefit various fields, such as bioinformatics, social network analysis, and neuroscience.

article: Data-driven decision-making consequential to individuals raises important questions of accountability and justice. Indeed, European law provides individuals limited rights to 'meaningful information about the logic' behind significant, autonomous decisions such as loan approvals, insurance quotes, and CV filtering. We undertake three experimental studies examining people's perceptions of justice in algorithmic decision-making under different scenarios and explanation styles. Dimensions of justice previously observed in response to human decision-making appear similarly engaged in response to algorithmic decisions. Qualitative analysis identified several concerns and heuristics involved in justice perceptions including arbitrariness, generalisation, and (in) dignity. Quantitative analysis indicates that explanation styles primarily matter to justice perceptions only when subjects are exposed to multiple different styles - under repeated exposure of one style, scenario effects obscure any explanation effects. Our results suggests there may be no 'best' approach to explaining algorithmic decisions, and that reflection on their automated nature both implicates and mitigates justice dimensions.

article: We study a bad arm existing checking problem in which a player's task is to judge whether a positive arm exists or not among given K arms by drawing as small number of arms as possible. Here, an arm is positive if its expected loss suffered by drawing the arm is at least a given threshold. This problem is a formalization of diagnosis of disease or machine failure. An interesting structure of this problem is the asymmetry of positive and negative (non-positive) arms' roles; finding one positive arm is enough to judge existence while all the arms must be discriminated as negative to judge non-existence. We propose an algorithms with arm selection policy (policy to determine the next arm to draw) and stopping condition (condition to stop drawing arms) utilizing this asymmetric problem structure and prove its effectiveness theoretically and empirically.

article: While the first amendment protects free speech, expression, religion, press, and assembly, there are some exceptions made for the sake of public safety and well being. Such examples include speech intending to incite violence, slanderlibel, threats intending to cause fear, and child pornography. These bans are quite reasonable and promote well being within society. The supreme court ruled that "obscene" content is not protected speech, and therefore illegal as "obscenity." This was a result of a hardcore pornographic studio that would mail out graphic porn ads, which deeply offended an older woman. In this case, I can understand how this is a problem. A business is distributing shocking imagery to people that do not wish to see it. Something should be done about it. The response by the supreme court, however, is inadequate at solving the problem. They ruled that obscene content is not protected speech. Speech is deemed "obscene" if it meets these 3 conditions: 1. Whether the average person, applying contemporary community standards," would find that the work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest, 2. Whether the work depicts or describes, in an offensive way, sexual conduct or excretory functions, as specifically defined by applicable state law 3. Whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. 1.Basically means that the majority of people believe that the work is intended for sexual arousal. 2.Means that the majority believe that the work depicts sexual content in an offensive way 3.Is self explanatory. The problem with 2 and 3 is that they're subjective. For example, some people may find gay porn extremely offensive. If this number was great enough within a particular community (such as a heavily religious town), someone could, in theory, be arrested for watching gay pornography. This of course never happens, because society doesn't find it offensive enough to ban it. This leads to the next problem-people aren't actually protected from obscene material like the law intends. For example, many "shocker" porn sites aren't shut down, as they aren't offensive enough to be, as set by point 2. However, these sites are intended to provide shock content, which is exactly what obscenity intends to prevent. With 3, "literary or artistic value" is very subjective. There are some very bizarre things regarded as art, there is no standard for art-that is the very nature of it. Thus, to say something lacks artistic or literary value is a mere matter of opinion, thus leading to a mob mentality. The supreme court actually revisited this case, and ruled in a 5-4 decision that obscene speech is still illegal even if it isn't distributed to minors or non consenting individuals. So the concept of simply viewing obscene material is incriminating. Because obscenity bans content, rather than the concept of distributing shocking content without warning, only the most offensive content gets banned. This leads to the Christopher Handley case. Christopher was arrested for mail ordering comic books that contained drawings of fictional characters that appeared to be childlike in physical appearance, engaging in sexual acts. The works were entirely fictional-mere drawings, and they accounted for only a small portion of his comic book collection. A raid of his residence did not result in finding any real CP. This content led to his arrest, as it is so extremely offensive. He ended up pleading guilty, as the lawyer suggested the jury would not change the ruling, and he did not want the jury to have to see the images. This is one of the few cases in which obscenity is enforced. While the content itself was harmless, as it was pure fiction, it led to an arrest and the waste of taxpayer money. He did not try to spam it to "trigger" people, he didn't send it to children. But he was still charged with obscenity. To summarize -Obscenity laws fail to protect individuals from "triggering" content, as intended. -Obscenity laws restrict harmless freedom of expression, and lead to controversial works being censored. -Obscenity laws are unclear, and can theoretically punish someone for something as subtle as watching gay porn.

article: I had only been a soldier for a month, and I clearly lacked the skills my father had. He had been knighted in just 3 months. In comparison, I could only hope to hold onto my job. My morals prevented me from carrying out the kind of cold-blooded orders a soldier had to. But this would be the first battle I had come face-to-face to. And I was determined to prove anyone who ever doubted me wrong. I saw the line of soldiers moving out. I wanted to move, but I resisted doing so. Something told me that I would get stomped apart by a powerful chariot, or slashed apart by the blessed blade of a quick moving bishop. The time dragged by and I stood my ground, not moving a single inch. Other soldiers were utilized as meat shields. Bishops dashed across the battleground, skewering their enemies. Chariots lurched forward, leaving a trail of destruction in its wake. The legendary Queen warriors crushed their opposition with ease. But I could tell that this would not go very well. The body count was too high on our side, and we never received reinforcements. Then I saw my chance - an opening on the field. I raced forward. It felt like time stopped. Nobody else moved, save for another soldier on the opposing side. I skidded to a stop, adjacent to the enemy soldier. A word flashed through my mind. [ En passant. ] (https: en.wikipedia.orgwikiEnpassant) I felt my blade moving. A twirl. My blade ate through flesh. Blood sprayed into the air, but I continued to move forward. Then I was in the thick of enemy lines. I had gone as far as I could go. 800 meters. The enemy was all around me. But I felt something surging within me. A primordial call. A promotion. I felt myself begin to grow, although it could have just been my imagination. I turned to face them. I had become one of the greats. Something surged within me. It was time to end this charade. article: It made sense that they weren't allowed in but that didn't change tuberculosis. Crawling through a forgotten storm drain, Sarah practically dragged Joseph along. His profuse coughing had become a tired death-rattle, which bounced pathetically off the walls of the claustrophobic space. It was nearly too dark to see, but Sarah knew that both of their clothes were streaked with the mould and rot that covered the perimeter of the drain. They would stick out like anything now, if they already wouldn't have before. At least it wasn't raining. Joseph was the hunter. If he died, then so did she. She couldn't catch or clean rabbits or squirrels like he could, all she could do was read the book. "COUGH COUGH." He sounded worse. As panic took control, Sarah sped up her crawl along the slimy floor, to weak wheezes of protest behind her. She didn't care, he would thank her when they got through. Through the darkness, she could see rusted out remains of a steel grille. They were under the walls. The drain widened, and Sarah got to her feet, carrying Joseph up with her. She looked up, and through the two holes in the manhole cover, she could see stars. "Joseph, I'm going to give you a boost." Above, in the Liberated City, darkness well concealed the two dirt-splattered orphans emerging from the sewers. Sarah looked around the city, it was just as ugly at night as it was during the day. Only a few lights lit up the city at night, resources were too precious to waste. Lights lined the wall, the lanterns dotted a huge oval through the darkness, tracing the boundaries of the city like purposefully scattered stars. "Whose there?" A uniform emerged from the darkness and began walking toward them. Sarah grabbed her half-conscious friend, "Joseph run!" The two started to make an escape down the street, but Joseph almost immediately shuffled to a halt and doubled over coughing and cringing with pain. The policeman approached, "It's past curfew and you need to- heavens what happened to your clothes." The officer looked at the two pathetically soaked kids, and Sarah's heart began to drop as the mans eyes followed the glistening trail they had left, winding all the way back into the sewer. "Miss, what is your name?" Sarah froze, she grasped for any name, any lie, there were a million names, and yet the one her mouth chose to involuntarily spit out was the real one. "Sarah." Even in the darkness she saw the mans face lose color. "Come with me Sarah." The officer hurriedly shuffled the strange children into one of the nearby buildings, an ugly brick townhouse. Once they were inside, the policeman turned on the lights and sat down heavily at his dinner table. Sarah nervously spoke first, "Where are you taking us sir?" The man didn't look at her, he looked like he was thinking. "This is my home." Joseph coughed quietly, it sounded like there was nothing left for him to give. They couldn't move anywhere else. "Please..... my friend his dying, we never would have come if it hadn't been life or death." The officer didn't seem as scary as he had in the dimly lit street. He had the kind of face that you couldn't be scared of, and kind eyes. The man looked scared, and ran a nervous hand through his hair. "I could be executed for harboring you two." Sarah didn't know what to say, but instead of feeling bad, she became angry. She frowned and shook with exhaustion from her hour long ordeal in the tunnel. She needed this man's help, but she snapped at him, "We can't help the way we were born! The city abandoned us! We're kids, how are we supposed to stay alive by ourselves?" The policeman looked up at her now, "Be quieter, the neighbors will hear." Sarah looked down, and bit her lip angrily. The man was risking his life. The officer spoke again, "I didn't know think were any of you still left out there. The last ones they found died a year ago." Joseph's parents. Hers had been gone for five years. "Were they executed?" Neither of them had ever known for sure. "Of course. They almost converted their jailers the first night they were caught, they couldn't be allowed to live." Sarah almost smiled. She remembered the night that Peter and Jessica had been taken away by the raiding party. They had died fighting the good fight. And now it seemed she would as well. Outside the house she could hear an alarm begin to wail. The policeman looked down in despair, "You did wake a neighbor, or someone saw you from the wall." Sarah thought about running for it, but she would be trapped the second she went back into the sewers. And Joseph would die if they ran. The call of a speaker outside cut through alarm, "COME OUT WITH YOUR HANDS UP. DO NOT RUN, THE EXITS ARE COVERED AND WE WILL SHOOT." Tears began to roll down Sarah's cheeks as she thought about their campsite in the woods, and the thin blanket covering her books. After she was gone, it would only take on rainfall to destroy the pages. The last book of the last religion on Earth would be erased, and the end of an era would finally come to pass. Maybe it would be for the better, the God Wars had killed billions and poisoned the Earth forever. But something would be missing. She couldn't quite tell you what, but as she looked around the policeman's home on her way out of the door she thought she might know what it was. Boring brick, cot bed, two or three white flowers in a dull vase on the small dining room table. There was no life, no humanity. She walked out of the door and dozens of men fell onto her and cuffed her hands. Then they went in for Joseph.

article: Hamiltonian cycles in graphs were first studied in the 1850s. Since then, an impressive amount of research has been dedicated to identifying classes of graphs that allow Hamiltonian cycles, and to related questions. The corresponding decision problem, that asks whether a given graph is Hamiltonian (i.e. admits a Hamiltonian cycle), is one of Karp's famous NP-complete problems. It remains NP-complete on planar cubic graphs. In this paper we study graphs of bounded degree that are far from being Hamiltonian, where a graph G on n vertices is far from being Hamiltonian, if modifying a constant fraction of n edges is necessary to make G Hamiltonian. We exhibit classes of graphs of bounded degree that are locally Hamiltonian , i.e. every subgraph induced by the neighbourhood of a small vertex set appears in some Hamiltonian graph, but that are far from being Hamiltonian. We then use these classes to obtain a lower bound in property testing. We show that in the bounded-degree graph model, Hamiltonicity is not testable with one-sided error probability and query complexity o (n). This contrasts the known fact that on planar (or minor-free) graph classes, Hamiltonicity is testable with constant query complexity in the bounded-degree graph model with two-sided error. Our proof is an intricate construction that shows how to turn a d -regular graph into a graph that is far from being Hamiltonian, and we use d -regular expander graphs to maintain local Hamiltonicity.

article: Recently, the precise performance of the Generalized LASSO algorithm for recovering structured signals from compressed noisy measurements, obtained via i.i.d. Gaussian matrices, has been characterized. The analysis is based on a framework introduced by Stojnic and heavily relies on the use of Gordon's Gaussian min-max theorem (GMT), a comparison principle on Gaussian processes. As a result, corresponding characterizations for other ensembles of measurement matrices have not been developed. In this work, we analyze the corresponding performance of the ensemble of isotropically random orthogonal (i.r.o.) measurements. We consider the constrained version of the Generalized LASSO and derive a sharp characterization of its normalized squared error in the large-system limit. When compared to its Gaussian counterpart, our result analytically confirms the superiority in performance of the i.r.o. ensemble. Our second result, derives an asymptotic lower bound on the minimum conic singular values of i.r.o. matrices. This bound is larger than the corresponding bound on Gaussian matrices. To prove our results we express i.r.o. matrices in terms of Gaussians and show that, with some modifications, the GMT framework is still applicable.

article: A network model is considered where Poisson distributed base stations transmit to N power-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) users (UEs) each that employ successive interference cancellation (SIC) for decoding. We propose three models for the clustering of NOMA UEs and consider two different ordering techniques for the NOMA UEs: mean signal power-based and instantaneous signal-to-intercell-interference-and-noise-ratio-based. For each technique, we present a signal-to-interference-and-noise ratio analysis for the coverage of the typical UE. We plot the rate region for the two-user case and show that neither ordering technique is consistently superior to the other. We propose two efficient algorithms for finding a feasible resource allocation that maximize the cell sum rate R tot, for general N, constrained to: 1) a minimum throughput T for each UE, 2) identical throughput for all UEs. We show the existence of: 1) an optimum N that maximizes the constrained R tot given a set of network parameters, 2) a critical SIC level necessary for NOMA to outperform orthogonal multiple access. The results highlight the importance in choosing the network parameters N, the constraints, and the ordering technique to balance the R tot and fairness requirements. We also show that interference-aware UE clustering can significantly improve performance.

article: Part of it is that lions get lots of exercise and don't eat very often. Have you ever seen a fat lion? Well, not counting ones in zoos. We can eat pretty much anything, anywhere, and if we couldn't, we wouldn't be able to support our big brains during a small famine. In theory all animals could produce all the nutrients their bodies need from any food, but in practise evolution takes shortcuts so certain animals require certain diets. A good example of this is vitamin C. Almost all animals can create their own vitamin C, but apes (including humans) can't. How did this happen? Apes have a diet that's high in vitamin C. At some point millions of years ago a mutation meant that an ape stopped being able to produce vitamin C, but because they already got a lot of vitamin C in their diet it didn't affect them negatively (maybe it even gave them a slight advantage because their body didn't need to spend energy producing vitamin C any more). In the end that ape's descendants went on to evolve into humans, who still require vitamin C in their diet because of that. On the other hand maybe another animal evolved a new way to breakdown certain foods (eg. meat) into even more useful nutrients, at which point that animal starts eat more of that food and becomes more specialised (by evolving from an omnivore into a carnivore),Cats are "hypercarnivores" - animals that only eat meat. article: dusts off pharmaceutical patent essay from last year in college A patent is a legal instrument which gives you the exclusive right to manufacture and sell something for a certain length of time. In order to get filed a patent has to show'inventiveness' (you've invented something new) and originality (it can't have been invented by someone else previously). The patent gives you a'negative right' - you have no obligation to make or sell your product, but you can force other people to not sell it (or to charge a fee for selling it). Say you invent the nail clipper. Before, everybody has been biting their nails, there has been no way to cut fingernails before. You could patent: A hinged metal cutting device [like this] (URL0) '. A hinged metal cutting device for the purpose of removing fingernails'. You can patent devices and methodsprocesses, but not ideas. As far as I'm aware the line between a method and an idea can be very blurry. There are different levels of patents. The first patent would stop anyone from manufacturing and selling nail clippers. It is the stronger of the two patents, because you have complete control over the invention. The second patent does not stop people from selling nail clippers, only from selling clippers for the purpose of clipping nails. A competitor could sell their own version of the nail clippers, but only if they said on the packet'not for fingernails! Only use on (X) '. Patents usually last for 20 years or so, from the date of filing. This is important in medicine and pharmaceuticals because you have to patent an invention before it is submitted to the FDA for approval. Since this approval can take many years you might have only a short space of time to sell your device. After the patent has expired anybody could make your device and sell it at whatever price they like. There are also jurisdictional issues: patents have to be filed separately in the US, the EU, Japan, and the rest of the world. If you have only filed a patent in the US a competitor could sell your device in the EU. Before a patent is filed the invention must be kept secret, but after it's filed you must make all the details of the invention public.," "Patents usually have a lifetime of 20 years. So if you had a patent for something, only you have the right to produce and sell it in that period. As soon as your patent wears out, anyone else can begin producing the exact same item. I'm not sure when the line is crossed and a patent is violated, leave that to the lawyers. But the idea stated above is the general concept.

Wires, shiny copper wires everywhere. There wasn't any more blood, apparently in deep cuts like this there wasn't enough blood to properly bleed. So I tried to clean it out myself which was really hard since touching those wires felt good. I had to resist the urge to pull some of them out. I bandaged my arm and then took some painkillers and went to sleep. The day after I woke up, once I remembered my new situation, I opened up the gauss pad to see if it had gotten better, but instead, it had gotten much much worse. The skin around the wound had started to melt as if it was no longer alive, the smell was horrendous, so I called my good friend Kyle, the doctor, and asked him if I could have a private appointment. From the sound of my voice, Kyle obviously knew something was up, so he told me to swing by his clinic at ten pm. Once I arrived, I told him to grab a seat and told the truth. It wasn't until I showed him the arm that he said "Geeze, I thought you were having a psychotic episode or something, but this..... this is real isn't it?" Then after examining the wound, he confirmed that which I already knew, that the skin around it was dying and that it was spreading fast. He then told me he'd need a sample of those wires to know what they were. As he looked at me, I felt a surge of strange thoughts start to course through my head, but I simply nooded and he got to work on getting one of those out. As he started pulling, I tensed up and he tried to ease up on the procedure. After it was done, he apologized for being so blunt and that he didn't know they were that sensitive. I could again only nod at his words. But he'd been wrong about the pain, what I had felt when he pulled it out was a pure and unbrideled sense of exctasy. It was absolute bliss to have it pulled. So while he went over the microscope, I was trying to hide my sudden erection under my coat. It had literarly been one of the most fundamentally rewarding and satisfying feeelings and sensations I'd ever felt in my whole life. But I was interrupted in my thoughts by a strange gurgling sound. When I looked up to where Kyle was standing, I could see that he was bleeding from a hole in his neck, as I watched him he slumped over on the floor and a big blood puddle started forming under his body. Then I saw the wire come crawling out of his body and I knew that it had killed him to protect itself. Now I'm sitting here in a corner in the building, waiting for the police to show up, I've told them everything and even if they don't believe me, they still have to come here and investigate. The wound is spreading more and more over my body, but I don't care about that anymore because of the feeling the new exposed wiring is giving me, it's like the air is singing to it. As more and more of it vanishes, I start feeling more alive, more in tune with my new self a self that only wants to pick.... pull.... pick and pull.... article: The cold hard stone floor was empty, save a pile of red cloth in the middle of the room. More specifically: a red night gown. The room was gloomy. The only source light was the moon light, creating square patterns on the floor the shape of windows. He lit a candle. The room was gloomy and dark, but felt safer with the orange light flickering throughout the room. He took a a large sip from his glass and felt the heat flow through his body. The little night gown moved. He downed the rest of his glass and stared at her. She was fiddling with her hair. Her blond locks were hanging in front of her face clumsily grasped by her small weak hands. "Has she ever seen her own hair before?" he wondered. He let go off the thought after realizing that such small everyday discoveries for a small child was never to be witnessed by him again. He filled his glass again, this time to the rim. "Daddy?" she said. Staring at him with endless curiosity and awe. "yes my love?" He smiled. It was not a sad smile. It was a smile of pure love and appreciation. "I am tired." He downed his glass. He felt the liquor burn in his throat. "I know dear, but you only have to be awake for a tiny bit longer." She gave him a look of confusion but didn't speak again. He continued. "I just wan na see you one last.." He held back a tear. "One last time before you go to bed..." The next few minutes he just sat there watching his daughter. She crawled around touching anything within her reach. Every move presented a new discovery, something new and fascinating she could explore. A blanket, a chair and a flower in the corner of the living room. He spoke up again. "I have lived and discovered, for quite a few years. Not like you. You have plenty years ahead of you. Do you understand?" Of course she didn't understand, but he knew that very well. He kept talking, in an attempt to find some comfort in his own words. "I love you. Good luck dear." His daughters playtime came to a sudden end as she turned her head facing the door at the other side of the room. "am I interrupting?" The voice was dark, but oddly comforting." "no, I was just finished" Death no longer scared him, not the idea of dying, nor the creature. It continued speaking. "Are you ready?" He hesitated. "Yes I am." the tall dark creature appeared in front of him., barely visible against the shadows. Strangely it felt better meeting Death in the dark. In darkness you did not have to look him in the eyes, or behold his strange features. The creature crossed the room and stopped in front of his daughter. A sudden sense of panic struck him. "Do not touch her! We had a deal!" "Yes, and I will honor our agreement." He nodded in response his eyes locked on the child. "But as you understand I am intrigued and fascinated by the living." Death stood still and stared upon his daughter for a while before he spoke again. "Now if you please, my time is precious." He stood up straight with his chin held high. "Take me with you, I am ready." All of sudden he felt no fear anymore. He was ready to meet his destiny." He crossed the room and stopped besides death. Death opened his hand and held it out into the shadows. "After you my friend" He started walking, and took one last glance over his shoulder. He watched his daughter sitting quietly on the floor, innocent and oblivious. He walked into the darkness with death by his side, into nothing."

article: With the increasing demands for privacy protection, many privacy-preserving machine learning systems were proposed in recent years. However, most of them cannot be put into production due to their slow training and inference speed caused by the heavy cost of homomorphic encryption and secure multiparty computation (MPC) methods. To circumvent this, I proposed a privacy definition which is suitable for large amount of data in machine learning tasks. Based on that, I showed that random transformations like linear transformation and random permutation can well protect privacy. Merging random transformations and arithmetic sharing together, I designed a framework for private machine learning with high efficiency and low computation cost.
